# Setup

This section loads all packages required for the full analysis pipeline and sets global options. Running this chunk first ensures a clean, reproducible environment — any missing packages are installed automatically so the script runs on any machine without manual preparation.

The pipeline draws on four groups of packages: data access (`cbsodataR`, `httr`, `jsonlite`, `readxl`), data wrangling (`dplyr`, `tidyr`, `stringr`, `janitor`), spatial analysis (`sf`, `nngeo`, `units`), econometric estimation (`fixest`, `lmtest`, `sandwich`, `spdep`), visualisation (`ggplot2` and companions), and output formatting (`modelsummary`, `stargazer`).

```{r packages}
required_packages <- c(
  "cbsodataR", # Data access
  "httr",
  "jsonlite",
  "readxl",
  "dplyr", # Data wrangling
  "tidyr",
  "stringr",
  "janitor",
  "sf", # Spatial
  "nngeo",
  "units",
  "fixest", # Fast FE estimation + clustered SEs
  "lmtest", # Modelling (used in later sections)
  "sandwich",
  "spdep",
  "spatialreg",
  "splines",
  "ggplot2", # Visualization
  "ggeffects",
  "scales",
  "viridis",
  "patchwork",
  "stargazer", # Output
  "modelsummary",
  "kableExtra",
  "webshot2"
)

new_pkgs <- required_packages[!(required_packages %in% installed.packages()[, "Package"])] # Finding the packages that are missing (not yet installed on the machine)
if (length(new_pkgs) > 0) {
  install.packages(new_pkgs, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org") # Installing only what is missing
}

invisible(lapply(required_packages, library, character.only = TRUE)) # Loops over every package in required_packages and calls library() on each one to load it into the R session (character.only = TRUE is needed because library() normally expects you to type a name directly, but here it is a vector). invisible() stops R from printing the package load confirmations.
```

```{r global-settings}
set.seed(42) # makes any random operations reproducible
```

# CBS Data: Download and Clean

## Downloading the CBS Kerncijfers

The primary data source is the *Kerncijfers Wijken en Buurten* published annually by Statistics Netherlands (CBS). Each edition covers all Dutch wijken (districts) and provides harmonised variables on housing valuations, household composition, income, employment, school infrastructure, and car ownership. We download eight annual editions (2016–2023) via the CBS Open Data API using the `cbsodataR` package and stack them into a balanced panel.

A few practical notes on the download function `download_kwb()`:

- **Caching:** each year is saved as a local RDS file after the first download. On subsequent runs the function loads from cache rather than re-downloading, which saves time and reduces API load. To force a fresh download, delete the relevant `data/raw/cbs_YYYY_raw.rds` file.
- **Column name harmonisation:** CBS occasionally renames variables across editions (e.g. the school distance variable is `AfstandTotSchool_` in some years and `AfstandTotBasisschool_` in others; income uses two different column names). The `grab()` helper function resolves this by matching on regex patterns rather than exact names.
- **Missing value codes:** CBS encodes suppressed values (suppressed for privacy when a district is too small) as −99997, −99998, or −99999. These are recoded to `NA`.
- **Car ownership:** `PersonenautoSPerHuishouden_` gives the average number of registered passenger cars per household in the wijk — added as part of the car ownership extension.

```{r cbs-download, cache=FALSE} 
# cashing is disabled
# ── CBS table IDs per year (Kerncijfers Wijken en Buurten) ──────────────────
cbs_table_ids <- c( # creates a named vector (year paired with a CBS API)
  "2016" = "83487NED",
  "2017" = "83765NED",
  "2018" = "84286NED",
  "2019" = "84583NED",
  "2020" = "84799NED",
  "2021" = "85039NED",
  "2022" = "85318NED",
  "2023" = "85618NED"
)

MISSING_CODES <- c(-99997, -99998, -99999) # CBS uses these specific numbers to represent suppressed or missing data
PANEL_RDS     <- "data/raw/cbs_panel_raw.rds" # stores the file path for the combined panel as a variable; used later to check if the panel already exists and to save it

# ── Helper: download and standardise one year ───────────────────────────────
download_kwb <- function(yr, table_id) { # Function definition; takes two inputs: yr (a year like "2018") and table_id (the CBS code like "84286NED")
  yr_rds <- paste0("data/raw/cbs_", yr, "_raw.rds")
  if (file.exists(yr_rds)) { # If the cache file for this year already exists on disk, load it and immediately return it; return() exits the function early with the cached data
    message("  ", yr, ": loaded from cache.")
    return(readRDS(yr_rds))
  }
  message("  ", yr, ": downloading (", table_id, ") ...") # If no cache found, "downloading" and call cbs-get-data() from the cbsodataR 
  raw <- cbs_get_data(table_id) |>
    mutate(across(where(is.character), str_trim)) |> # Applies str_trim() to every character column (removes any leading or trailing spaces from text values)
    filter(str_starts(WijkenEnBuurten, "WK")) |> # Keeps only districts (wijken)
    mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ ifelse(. %in% MISSING_CODES, NA, .))) # Replace missing codes with NA
  nms <- names(raw) # Store column names

  # Grab first column matching pattern; return NA vector if absent
  grab <- function(pat) {
    col <- grep(pat, nms, value = TRUE)[1]
    if (is.na(col)) rep(NA_real_, nrow(raw)) else raw[[col]]
  }

  # Column names that differ across years
  dist_col   <- if (any(grepl("^AfstandTotSchool_", nms))) "^AfstandTotSchool_"
                else "^AfstandTotBasisschool_" # Check which version exists in the current year's data, if at least one column matches, returns TRUE
  income_col <- if (any(grepl("^GemGestandaardiseerdInkomenVanHuish_", nms)))
                  "^GemGestandaardiseerdInkomenVanHuish_"
                else "^GemiddeldGestandaardiseerdInkomenVanHuishoudens_"
  pct_single_direct <- any(grepl("^PercentageEenpersoonshuishoudens_", nms)) # Checks whether CBS directly provides the percentage of single-person households in this year

  hh_total  <- grab("^HuishoudensTotaal_") # Pre-fetch household count columns
  hh_single <- grab("^Eenpersoonshuishoudens_")

  out <- tibble( # Build the output tibble (one raw per district)
    year                = as.integer(yr), # "2018" to 2018 (string to number)
    wijk_code           = raw$WijkenEnBuurten,
    gemeente_code       = paste0("GM", str_sub(raw$WijkenEnBuurten, 3, 6)), # Extracts the municipality code from the district code. Wijk codes look like "WK034401", where characters 3–6 ("0344") are the municipality number; prepending "GM" gives the standard CBS municipality code "GM0344"
    woz_avg_k           = grab("^GemiddeldeWOZWaardeVanWoningen_"), # Other columns call grab() with the appropriate pattern to retrieve that CBS variable
    dist_primary_school = grab(dist_col),
    n_schools_3km       = grab("^ScholenBinnen3Km_"),
    hh_total            = hh_total,
    hh_single           = hh_single,
    hh_no_children      = grab("^HuishoudensZonderKinderen_"),
    hh_with_children    = grab("^HuishoudensMetKinderen_"),
    koopwoningen        = grab("^Koopwoningen_"),
    woningvoorraad      = grab("^Woningvoorraad_"),
    income_avg_k        = grab(income_col),
    pct_low_income      = grab("^HuishoudensMetEenLaagInkomen_"),
    pct_employed        = grab("^Nettoarbeidsparticipatie_"),
    pop_total           = grab("^AantalInwoners_"),
    pop_density_km2     = grab("^Omgevingsadressendichtheid_"),
    n_age_0_14          = grab("^k_0Tot15Jaar_"),
    cars_per_hh         = grab("^PersonenautoSPerHuishouden_")
  ) |>
  mutate( # Adds derived percentage columns
    pct_single_hh        = if (pct_single_direct) # If CBS provides the singles percentage directly (pct_single_direct = TRUE), use it
                             grab("^PercentageEenpersoonshuishoudens_")
                           else 100 * hh_single / hh_total, # If no, compute it
    pct_hh_no_children   = 100 * hh_no_children  / hh_total,
    pct_hh_with_children = 100 * hh_with_children / hh_total,
    pct_owner_occupied   = koopwoningen, # Just renamed
    pct_age_0_14         = 100 * n_age_0_14 / pop_total
  )

  saveRDS(out, yr_rds) # Save to cache and return
  out
}

# ── Download all years and stack into panel ─────────────────────────────────
if (file.exists(PANEL_RDS)) { # Check if full panel already cached
  cbs_panel <- readRDS(PANEL_RDS)
  message("Panel loaded from cache: ", nrow(cbs_panel), " rows")
} else {
  cbs_panel <- bind_rows(mapply(download_kwb, # If no cached panel exists, download all years and stack; mapply is like a loop — it calls download_kwb(yr="2016", table_id="83487NED"), then download_kwb(yr="2017", table_id="83765NED"), and so on
                                yr       = names(cbs_table_ids),
                                table_id = cbs_table_ids,
                                SIMPLIFY = FALSE)) # tells mapply to return a list of tibbles rather than trying to combine them into a matrix, bind_rows() then stacks all those tibbles into one tall panel
  saveRDS(cbs_panel, PANEL_RDS) # Save the full panel
  message("Panel built and cached: ", nrow(cbs_panel), " rows")
}

# 2023 cross-section kept as cbs_clean for EDA chunks below
cbs_clean <- cbs_panel %>% filter(year == 2023)
cat("Panel years:", paste(sort(unique(cbs_panel$year)), collapse = ", "), "\n") # Final diagnostics 
cat("Wijken (2023):", nrow(cbs_clean), "\n")
```

The output should confirm eight panel years (2016–2023) and approximately 3,350 wijken in the 2023 cross-section. The exact count varies slightly because CBS occasionally adds or merges wijken between editions.

## Data Overview

A quick `glimpse()` of the 2023 cross-section confirms column names, data types, and rough value ranges. This is a sanity check, we want to verify that numeric columns parsed correctly (no character columns where numbers are expected), that the CBS missing codes were recoded to `NA`, and that `cars_per_hh` is present with plausible values (roughly 0.8–1.8 for Dutch wijken).

```{r cbs-overview}
glimpse(cbs_clean) # Prints column names, data types, and a sample of values for the 2023 cross-section. The purpose is to visually confirm that numeric columns parsed correctly and that cars_per_hh is present
```

## Cleaning and Derived Variables

Several derived variables are added to the panel before any analysis. The most important are:

- **`log_woz`**: the natural log of average WOZ value (in euros, not thousands). The log transformation is standard in the hedonic pricing literature — it yields coefficients interpretable as percentage changes and compresses the right-skewed house price distribution.
- **`delta_singles_lag1`**: the one-year lagged change in single-person household share (Singlesᵢ,ₜ₋₁ − Singlesᵢ,ₜ₋₂). This is included in the panel models to control for prior demographic momentum — districts that were already gaining singles may have experienced anticipatory house price movements.
- **`gemeente_fe`**: a factor version of the municipality code, used as the fixed effect variable in cross-sectional models.

Note that `delta_singles_lag1` requires two prior years of data per wijk, so it is unavailable for 2016 and 2017 observations, those rows receive `NA` and are excluded from the panel models.

```{r cbs-clean}
# ── 1. Drop panel rows without a WOZ value ───────────────────────────────────
n_before   <- nrow(cbs_panel)
cbs_panel  <- cbs_panel %>% filter(!is.na(woz_avg_k))
cat("Dropped", n_before - nrow(cbs_panel), "panel rows with missing WOZ.\n")

# ── 2. Add derived variables to the full panel ────────────────────────────────
# delta_singles_lag1 = Singlesᵢ,ₜ₋₁ − Singlesᵢ,ₜ₋₂
# Requires at least 3 years of data per district; NA otherwise.
cbs_panel <- cbs_panel %>%
  arrange(wijk_code, year) %>% # Sort the data by wijk code first, then by year within each wijk (for lag())
  group_by(wijk_code) %>% # All subsequent operations should be done separately for each wijk
  mutate(
    log_woz            = log(woz_avg_k * 1000), # woz_avg_k is in thousands of euros, so multiplying by 1000 converts it back to euros before taking the log
    gemeente_fe        = factor(gemeente_code), # Converts from string, e.g. "GM0344", to factor variable (for categorical fixed effect)
    singles_std        = as.numeric(scale(pct_single_hh)), # Standardised pct_single_hh, used for exploratory analysis
    lag1_singles       = lag(pct_single_hh, 1),   # Singlesᵢ,ₜ₋₁
    lag2_singles       = lag(pct_single_hh, 2),   # Singlesᵢ,ₜ₋₂
    delta_singles_lag1 = lag1_singles - lag2_singles
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>% # Removes the grouping so subsequent operations apply to the whole data frame again, not separately per wijk
  select(-lag1_singles, -lag2_singles)  # intermediate columns no longer needed

# ── 3. Save panel and 2023 cross-section ─────────────────────────────────────
saveRDS(cbs_panel, "data/processed/cbs_panel.rds")

cbs_clean <- cbs_panel %>% filter(year == 2023)
saveRDS(cbs_clean, "data/processed/cbs_clean.rds")

# ── 4. Diagnostics ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
n_delta <- sum(!is.na(cbs_panel$delta_singles_lag1))
cat("Panel rows with delta_singles_lag1 available:", n_delta,
    "(out of", nrow(cbs_panel), ")\n")
cat("2023 cross-section:", nrow(cbs_clean), "districts\n")
```

**Output check:** the diagnostics confirm three expected results. Zero rows dropped for missing WOZ means the per-year caches already passed this filter on a previous run, loading from `PANEL_RDS` gives an already-clean panel. The `delta_singles_lag1` count of ~16,721 out of ~24,188 is correct because the variable requires two prior years of data: 2016 and 2017 rows are always NA (no lag available), leaving 6 years × ~2,800 wijken ≈ 16,800 valid observations. The 2023 cross-section of 3,232 wijken is consistent with all prior steps.


## Missingness Check

Before moving to modelling it is important to understand how much data is missing and why. This matters for two reasons: missing values reduce the regression sample size, and if missingness is systematic (e.g. always in small or rural districts) it could bias the estimates. We check all key analysis variables on the 2023 cross-section.

```{r cbs-missing}
key_vars <- c("woz_avg_k", "dist_primary_school", "n_schools_3km",
              "pct_single_hh", "pct_age_0_14", "pct_owner_occupied",
              "income_avg_k", "pct_employed", "pop_density_km2", "cars_per_hh")

cbs_clean %>% # Check of 2023 cross sectional data
  select(all_of(key_vars)) %>% # Selects listed above variables
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.)))) %>% # Counts NAs per column
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "n_missing") %>% # Each variable is a raw
  mutate(pct_missing = round(100 * n_missing / nrow(cbs_clean), 1)) %>% # Percentage of missing
  print()
```

The missingness pattern is exactly as expected and has a clear explanation for every variable:

- **`woz_avg_k`: 0** — by construction, since we filtered out rows without a WOZ value in the cleaning step.
- **`dist_primary_school`, `n_schools_3km`: 1 each** — negligible (essentially 0%), likely one unusually configured district. No action needed.
- **`pct_single_hh`, `pct_age_0_14`, `pct_owner_occupied`: 0** — fully observed, no concerns.
- **`income_avg_k`: 221 missing (6.8%) and `pct_employed`: 159 missing (4.9%)** — this is a known CBS privacy rule. For very small districts (typically fewer than 100–150 households), CBS suppresses income and employment figures to prevent identification of individual residents. This is not random missingness — it is concentrated in the smallest, most rural wijken. These will be dropped by listwise deletion when the regression sample is formed, which is acceptable given that we already exclude districts with fewer than 500 residents.
- **`cars_per_hh`: 133 missing (4.1%)** — same mechanism as income and employment. CBS suppresses car ownership figures for the smallest districts. Most of these overlap with the districts already excluded by the population filter.

# Spatial Join: School Distances

The CBS data provides `dist_primary_school`, the average distance from residential addresses in each wijk to the nearest primary school, as reported by CBS itself. This is our main proximity variable. However, as a robustness check we also compute our own distance measure from raw school coordinates, which allows us to verify the CBS figures and compute additional spatial variables (school density buffers, distances to good vs standard schools).

This section builds those spatial measures in three steps: (1) load wijk boundary polygons, (2) load DUO school point locations, (3) compute nearest-school distances and buffer counts.

All spatial objects are projected to **RD New (EPSG:28992)**, the Dutch national coordinate reference system. RD New uses metres as its unit, which means distance calculations are straightforward and accurate without any trigonometric correction. This is the standard CRS for Dutch geospatial work.

## Loading CBS District Shapefiles

The official CBS wijk boundary polygons are downloaded from PDOK (the Dutch national geodata platform). The chunk tries three sources in sequence, a paginated WFS GeoJSON download, and two versions of a CBS ZIP file — falling back to the next if the previous fails. This makes the script resilient to URL changes, which happen occasionally as CBS updates its data portal.

After loading, the district code column is standardised to `WijkBuurtcode` regardless of how it was named in the source file, and the object is saved locally so the download only runs once.

```{r shapefiles, cache=TRUE}
message("Loading CBS wijk shapefile ...")

# ── Load from local cache if available ───────────────────────────────────────
wijken_sf <- NULL # Code below checks is.null(wijken_sf) to decide whether a download is needed
if (file.exists("data/raw/wijken_sf.rds")) { # Check the local cache
  tmp <- readRDS("data/raw/wijken_sf.rds") # Load the cache
  if (inherits(tmp, "sf") && nrow(tmp) > 0) { # 2 checks: actually spatial(sf) object; at least 1 row of data
    wijken_sf <- tmp # If the cache passed validation, assign it to wijken_sf and print a confirmation 
    message("Loaded wijken_sf from local cache: ", nrow(wijken_sf), " features")
  } else { # Reject a bad cache
    message("Cache found but not a valid sf object — re-downloading ...")
  }
}

# ── Download if cache not available ──────────────────────────────────────────
# Attempt 1: PDOK WFS via paginated GeoJSON download (1000 features per page)
if (is.null(wijken_sf)) tryCatch({
  message("Trying PDOK WFS GeoJSON download (paginated) ...")
  wfs_base <- paste0(
    "https://service.pdok.nl/cbs/wijkenbuurten/2023/wfs/v1_0", # Build the base URL
    "?SERVICE=WFS&VERSION=2.0.0&REQUEST=GetFeature", # The URL is split across multiple strings just for readability
    "&TYPENAMES=wijken&OUTPUTFORMAT=application%2Fjson",
    "&COUNT=1000"
  )
  pages <- list() # List that will collect each batch of 1000 features
  start <- 0 # Index of the first feature to request. It starts at 0 and increments by 1000 each loop
  repeat { # Start the download loop
    url <- paste0(wfs_base, "&STARTINDEX=", start)
    tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".json")
    httr::GET(url, httr::timeout(120), httr::write_disk(tmp, overwrite = TRUE))
    page <- st_read(tmp, quiet = TRUE)
    if (nrow(page) == 0) break
    pages[[length(pages) + 1]] <- page
    message("  Downloaded ", start + nrow(page), " features so far ...")
    if (nrow(page) < 1000) break
    start <- start + 1000
  }
  wijken_sf <- do.call(rbind, pages)
  message("PDOK WFS GeoJSON succeeded: ", nrow(wijken_sf), " features total.")
}, error = function(e) message("Attempt 1 failed: ", e$message))

# Attempt 2: CBS ZIP — 2023 version 1
if (is.null(wijken_sf) || nrow(wijken_sf) == 0) {
  tryCatch({
    message("Trying CBS ZIP download (v1) ...")
    zip_url  <- "https://www.cbs.nl/-/media/cbs/dossiers/nederland-regionaal/wijk-en-buurtstatistieken/2023/shape-2023-versie-1-0.zip"
    zip_path <- "data/raw/wijken_2023.zip"
    download.file(zip_url, zip_path, mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE)
    unzip(zip_path, exdir = "data/raw/wijken_2023", overwrite = TRUE)
    shp_file <- list.files("data/raw/wijken_2023", pattern = "\\.shp$",
                           full.names = TRUE, recursive = TRUE)
    wijken_sf <- st_read(shp_file[1], quiet = TRUE) %>%
      filter(grepl("^WK", WK_CODE))
    message("CBS ZIP v1 succeeded.")
  }, error = function(e) message("Attempt 2 failed: ", e$message))
}

# Attempt 3: CBS ZIP — 2023 version 2
if (is.null(wijken_sf) || nrow(wijken_sf) == 0) {
  tryCatch({
    message("Trying CBS ZIP download (v2) ...")
    zip_url  <- "https://www.cbs.nl/-/media/cbs/dossiers/nederland-regionaal/wijk-en-buurtstatistieken/2023/shape-2023-versie-2-0.zip"
    zip_path <- "data/raw/wijken_2023_v2.zip"
    download.file(zip_url, zip_path, mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE)
    unzip(zip_path, exdir = "data/raw/wijken_2023_v2", overwrite = TRUE)
    shp_file <- list.files("data/raw/wijken_2023_v2", pattern = "\\.shp$",
                           full.names = TRUE, recursive = TRUE)
    wijken_sf <- st_read(shp_file[1], quiet = TRUE) %>%
      filter(grepl("^WK", WK_CODE))
    message("CBS ZIP v2 succeeded.")
  }, error = function(e) message("Attempt 3 failed: ", e$message))
}

if (is.null(wijken_sf) || nrow(wijken_sf) == 0) {
  stop("All shapefile download attempts failed. The spatial robustness section will be skipped. ",
       "The main analysis can proceed using dist_primary_school from CBS.")
}

# Project to RD New
wijken_sf <- wijken_sf %>% st_transform(28992)

# Standardise the district code column name
code_col <- names(wijken_sf)[grepl("WK_CODE|WijkBuurtcode|statcode|wijkcode",
                                    names(wijken_sf), ignore.case = TRUE)][1]
wijken_sf <- wijken_sf %>% rename(WijkBuurtcode = all_of(code_col))

message("Wijken loaded: ", nrow(wijken_sf), " features | CRS: EPSG:28992")
saveRDS(wijken_sf, "data/raw/wijken_sf.rds")
```

## Loading DUO School Locations

DUO (Dienst Uitvoering Onderwijs) is the Dutch government agency responsible for education administration. It publishes open data on all registered schools, including geocoded addresses for primary schools (*hoofdvestigingen basisonderwijs*). We download the most recent file and convert it to an `sf` point object projected to RD New, so it is in the same CRS (Coordinate Reference System) as the wijk polygons and distances can be computed in metres.

The chunk handles three possible coordinate formats that DUO has used across different file versions: direct latitude/longitude columns, RD New x/y columns, and postcode-only (which requires geocoding via the PDOK Locatieserver API). This makes the download robust to future file format changes. Schools with a recorded closure date are dropped so only active schools are retained.

```{r duo-schools, cache=TRUE}
message("Downloading DUO primary school locations ...")

# Correct URL as of May 2026 (DUO restructured their open data portal)
duo_url  <- "https://duo.nl/open_onderwijsdata/images/01.-hoofdvestigingen-basisonderwijs.csv"
duo_path <- "data/raw/duo_po_hoofdvestigingen.csv"
download.file(duo_url, duo_path, mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE)
duo_raw <- read.csv2(duo_path, fileEncoding = "latin1", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

message("DUO columns: ", paste(names(duo_raw), collapse = ", "))

duo_schools <- NULL

has_latlon   <- all(c("LATITUDE", "LONGITUDE") %in% names(duo_raw))
has_rdnew    <- all(c("XCOORD", "YCOORD") %in% names(duo_raw))
has_postcode <- "POSTCODE" %in% names(duo_raw)

if (has_latlon) {
  duo_schools <- duo_raw %>%
    filter(!is.na(LATITUDE), !is.na(LONGITUDE), LATITUDE != 0) %>%
    st_as_sf(coords = c("LONGITUDE", "LATITUDE"), crs = 4326) %>%
    st_transform(28992)
  message("Used LATITUDE/LONGITUDE columns.")

} else if (has_rdnew) {
  duo_schools <- duo_raw %>%
    filter(!is.na(XCOORD), !is.na(YCOORD), XCOORD != 0) %>%
    st_as_sf(coords = c("XCOORD", "YCOORD"), crs = 28992)
  message("Used XCOORD/YCOORD columns.")

} else if (has_postcode) {
  # No direct coordinates — geocode via PDOK Locatieserver using postcode
  message("No coordinate columns found. Geocoding ", nrow(duo_raw),
          " schools via PDOK Locatieserver (postcode-level) ...")

  geocode_postcode <- function(pc) {
    pc <- gsub(" ", "", pc)
    if (is.na(pc) || nchar(pc) < 6) return(c(NA_real_, NA_real_))
    url <- paste0(
      "https://api.pdok.nl/bzk/locatieserver/search/v3_1/free",
      "?q=", URLencode(pc), "&rows=1&fq=type:postcode&fl=centroide_rd"
    )
    tryCatch({
      resp  <- httr::GET(url, httr::timeout(8))
      res   <- jsonlite::fromJSON(httr::content(resp, "text", encoding = "UTF-8"))
      if (res$response$numFound > 0) {
        pt <- res$response$docs$centroide_rd[1]
        xy <- as.numeric(strsplit(gsub("POINT\\(|\\)", "", pt), " ")[[1]])
        return(xy)
      }
    }, error = function(e) NULL)
    return(c(NA_real_, NA_real_))
  }

  # Deduplicate postcodes to minimise API calls
  pcs <- unique(duo_raw$POSTCODE)
  message("Unique postcodes to geocode: ", length(pcs))
  coords_list <- lapply(seq_along(pcs), function(i) {
    if (i %% 200 == 0) message("  ... ", i, " / ", length(pcs))
    Sys.sleep(0.05)   # ~20 req/s — stays well within PDOK limits
    xy <- geocode_postcode(pcs[i])
    data.frame(POSTCODE = pcs[i], x_rd = xy[1], y_rd = xy[2],
               stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  })
  pc_coords <- do.call(rbind, coords_list)

  duo_geo <- duo_raw %>%
    left_join(pc_coords, by = "POSTCODE") %>%
    filter(!is.na(x_rd), !is.na(y_rd))

  duo_schools <- duo_geo %>%
    st_as_sf(coords = c("x_rd", "y_rd"), crs = 28992)
  message("Geocoded ", nrow(duo_schools), " schools via PDOK postcode lookup.")

} else {
  message("Could not find or derive coordinates. Check DUO column names above.")
}

if (!is.null(duo_schools)) {
  # Drop schools that have been closed (if column present)
  close_col <- grep("OPHEFFING|EINDDATUM", names(duo_schools),
                    value = TRUE, ignore.case = TRUE)[1]
  if (!is.na(close_col)) {
    duo_schools <- duo_schools %>%
      filter(is.na(.data[[close_col]]) | .data[[close_col]] == "")
  }
  message("Active primary schools ready: ", nrow(duo_schools))
  saveRDS(duo_schools, "data/raw/duo_schools_sf.rds")
} else {
  message("DUO school data unavailable — spatial robustness check will be skipped.")
  message("Main analysis proceeds using dist_primary_school from CBS.")
}
```

## Computing Distance to Nearest School

For each wijk we need a single distance value, the distance from the wijk to its nearest primary school. Rather than computing a full distance matrix between all wijken and all schools (which would be ~3,300 × 6,000 = ~20 million pairs), we use `st_nn()` from the `nngeo` package, which implements a fast nearest-neighbour search. Setting `k = 1` retrieves only the single closest school per wijk.

The distance is measured from the **wijk centroid** (the geometric centre of the wijk polygon) to the nearest school point. This is our robustness measure (`dist_school_centroid_km`). The main proximity variable (`dist_primary_school` from CBS) is based on the average distance from all residential addresses in the wijk, which is a more precise measure but only available from CBS directly. The two measures should correlate strongly; any divergence between them in the robustness checks tells us something about how sensitive results are to the exact distance operationalisation.

```{r nearest-school, cache=TRUE}
if (is.null(duo_schools)) {
  message("Skipping nearest-school computation — DUO data unavailable.")
  wijken_centroids <- NULL
} else {
  # Compute district centroids
  wijken_centroids <- wijken_sf %>%
    st_centroid() %>%
    select(WijkBuurtcode)

  message("Computing nearest-school distances (may take ~30 seconds) ...")

  nn_result <- st_nn(
    x          = wijken_centroids,
    y          = duo_schools,
    k          = 1,
    returnDist = TRUE,
    progress   = TRUE
  )

  wijken_centroids$dist_school_centroid_km <- sapply(nn_result$dist, `[`, 1) / 1000

  cat("\nSummary — centroid-to-nearest-school distance (km):\n")
  print(summary(wijken_centroids$dist_school_centroid_km))
}
```
The distances are plausible for the Netherlands. A median of ~0.70 km means most wijk centroids are within walking distance of a school, expected in a densely built country. The mean (~1.01 km) is slightly higher than the median due to rural outliers, producing a mild right skew. The maximum (~11.5 km) corresponds to very remote rural districts in provinces like Drenthe or Zeeland. The minimum (~4 m) is a wijk centroid that falls essentially on top of a school building, which can happen in compact inner-city wijken.


## Counting Schools Within Radius Buffers

Distance to the nearest school captures proximity but not density — a wijk with one school 300m away and a wijk with five schools within 300m both get the same nearest-school distance. As a complementary measure we count how many schools fall within a 1 km radius buffer around each wijk centroid. The 1 km threshold is chosen because it is close to the mean CBS distance (~0.91 km). This school density measure is used in robustness checks and may capture the nuisance dimension (more schools = more traffic and noise) better than a single nearest-school distance.

The `st_buffer()` function draws a circle of the specified radius around each centroid point, and `st_intersects()` counts how many school points fall inside it.

```{r school-buffers, cache=TRUE}
if (is.null(wijken_centroids)) {
  message("Skipping school buffer counts — DUO data unavailable.")
  message("Spatial robustness check skipped; main analysis uses CBS dist_primary_school.")
} else {
  count_in_buffer <- function(pts, targets, radius_m) {
    lengths(st_intersects(st_buffer(pts, dist = radius_m), targets))
  }

  wijken_centroids$n_schools_1km  <- count_in_buffer(wijken_centroids, duo_schools, 1000)

  # Save spatial variables as a plain data frame (drop geometry)
  spatial_vars <- wijken_centroids %>%
    st_drop_geometry() %>%
    rename(wijk_code = WijkBuurtcode)

  saveRDS(spatial_vars, "data/processed/spatial_vars.rds")
  message("Spatial variables saved.")
}
```

## School Quality Classification

Not all schools are equal in the eyes of housing markets. Gibbons & Machin (2006) found that only the top-performing schools generate a price premium, for the remaining schools, proximity is either neutral or a mild discount due to externalities. To test this in the Dutch context, we classify each school as **good** (top 20% by standardised test score) or **standard** (bottom 80%) and compute separate distances to each type per wijk.

Dutch primary schools use the *doorstroomtoets* as a standardised exit test, but six different test providers exist (IEP, LVS, Route 8, DIA, AMN, DOE), each with its own scale. Directly comparing raw scores across providers would be meaningless, a score of 80 on one test is not the same as 80 on another. The solution is to **standardise within provider** first: for each provider, subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation. This puts all schools on a common scale (z-scores), after which a single global percentile rank is computed across all schools. Schools at or above the 80th percentile are flagged as `good_school = TRUE`.

The chunk picks the first non-missing, non-zero test score per school (some schools may appear in the file with scores from multiple providers or with zero placeholders) and deduplicates on BRIN code (the unique school identifier).

```{r school-quality-scoring}
# ── Download DUO doorstroomtoets scores 2023-2024 (pure base R) ──────────────
scores_url  <- "https://duo.nl/open_onderwijsdata/images/05.-gemiddelde-eindscores-bo-sbo-2023-2024.csv"
scores_path <- "data/raw/duo_eindscores_2023_2024.csv"
if (!file.exists(scores_path))
  download.file(scores_url, scores_path, mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE)

scores_raw <- read.csv2(scores_path, stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
                        check.names = FALSE, fileEncoding = "UTF-8-BOM")

test_cols <- c("IEP_GEM", "LIB_GEM", "ROUTE8_GEM", "DIA_GEM", "AMN_GEM", "DOE_GEM")
sc        <- scores_raw[, c("INSTELLINGSCODE", test_cols)]
for (col in test_cols) sc[[col]] <- as.numeric(gsub(",", ".", sc[[col]]))

# Pick first non-zero test score for each school
test_used <- character(nrow(sc))
raw_score <- numeric(nrow(sc))
for (i in seq_len(nrow(sc))) {
  v <- as.numeric(sc[i, test_cols])
  k <- which(!is.na(v) & v > 0)
  if (length(k)) { test_used[i] <- test_cols[k[1]]; raw_score[i] <- v[k[1]] }
  else            { test_used[i] <- NA_character_;   raw_score[i] <- NA_real_ }
}
sc$test_used <- test_used
sc$raw_score <- raw_score
sc <- sc[!is.na(sc$raw_score), c("INSTELLINGSCODE", "test_used", "raw_score")]
sc <- sc[!duplicated(sc$INSTELLINGSCODE), ]

# Standardise within provider, global percentile rank, top-20% flag
sc$score_std   <- ave(sc$raw_score, sc$test_used,
                      FUN = function(x) (x - mean(x)) / sd(x))
sc$score_pct   <- rank(sc$score_std, ties.method = "average") / nrow(sc)
sc$good_school <- sc$score_pct >= 0.80
scores_school  <- sc

cat("Schools scored:", nrow(scores_school), "\n")
cat("Good (top 20%):", sum(scores_school$good_school), "\n")
cat("Standard:", sum(!scores_school$good_school), "\n")
print(table(scores_school$test_used))
```

```{r school-quality-join}
# ── Attach quality flag to sf object using cbind() ───────────────────────────
if (!exists("duo_schools") || is.null(duo_schools))
  duo_schools <- readRDS("data/raw/duo_schools_sf.rds")

brin_col <- grep("INSTELLINGSCODE|BRIN", names(duo_schools),
                 ignore.case = TRUE, value = TRUE)[1]
cat("Joining on:", brin_col, "\n")

idx       <- match(duo_schools[[brin_col]], scores_school$INSTELLINGSCODE)
good_flag <- scores_school$good_school[idx]
good_flag[is.na(good_flag)] <- FALSE
pct_flag  <- scores_school$score_pct[idx]

# Reconstruct sf explicitly: drop geometry, add columns, reattach geometry
duo_df              <- sf::st_drop_geometry(duo_schools)
duo_df$good_school  <- good_flag
duo_df$score_pct    <- pct_flag
duo_schools_quality <- sf::st_sf(duo_df, geometry = sf::st_geometry(duo_schools))

good_schools_sf <- duo_schools_quality[duo_schools_quality$good_school,  ]
std_schools_sf  <- duo_schools_quality[!duo_schools_quality$good_school, ]

cat("class(good_schools_sf):", paste(class(good_schools_sf), collapse = ", "), "\n")
cat("Good school sf rows:", nrow(good_schools_sf), "\n")
cat("Standard school sf rows:", nrow(std_schools_sf), "\n")

cat("Good school locations matched:", nrow(good_schools_sf), "\n")
cat("Standard school locations matched:", nrow(std_schools_sf), "\n")
```

Both chunks ran correctly. 6,103 schools scored in total, of which 1,207 good and 4,791 standard locations were matched to the sf object (1,207 + 4,791 = 5,998 matched). This leaves 105 unmatched schools (6,103 − 5,998 = 105), a 1.7% non-match rate — still excellent overall. The unmatched schools are likely those that closed, merged, or changed BRIN codes between the doorstroomtoets scoring file and the geocoding file, both from DUO but from slightly different publication dates.

## Distances to Good and Standard Schools

```{r school-quality-distances, cache=TRUE}
library(nngeo)

# Ensure wijken_centroids is an sf object in memory
if (!exists("wijken_centroids") || is.null(wijken_centroids) ||
    !inherits(wijken_centroids, "sf")) {
  wijk_tmp <- readRDS("data/raw/wijken_sf.rds")
  if (!inherits(wijk_tmp, "sf")) {
    stop("wijken_sf.rds is a plain data frame — please run the 'shapefiles' ",
         "and 'nearest-school' chunks first to recreate wijken_centroids as an sf object.")
  }
  wijken_centroids <- sf::st_centroid(wijk_tmp) |>
                      dplyr::select(WijkBuurtcode)
  message("wijken_centroids reconstructed from wijken_sf.rds")
}

if (is.null(wijken_centroids) || nrow(good_schools_sf) == 0) {
  message("Skipping school quality distances — required data unavailable.")
} else {
  message("Computing distances to nearest good school ...")
  nn_good <- st_nn(wijken_centroids, good_schools_sf,
                   k = 1, returnDist = TRUE, progress = FALSE)

  message("Computing distances to nearest standard school ...")
  nn_std  <- st_nn(wijken_centroids, std_schools_sf,
                   k = 1, returnDist = TRUE, progress = FALSE)

  wijken_centroids$dist_good_school_km <- sapply(nn_good$dist, `[`, 1) / 1000
  wijken_centroids$dist_std_school_km  <- sapply(nn_std$dist,  `[`, 1) / 1000

  cat("Distance to nearest good school (km):\n")
  print(summary(wijken_centroids$dist_good_school_km))
  cat("\nDistance to nearest standard school (km):\n")
  print(summary(wijken_centroids$dist_std_school_km))

  # Append new columns to existing spatial_vars rather than overwriting
  new_cols <- data.frame(
    wijk_code           = wijken_centroids$WijkBuurtcode,
    dist_good_school_km = wijken_centroids$dist_good_school_km,
    dist_std_school_km  = wijken_centroids$dist_std_school_km
  )

  if (file.exists("data/processed/spatial_vars.rds")) {
    spatial_vars <- readRDS("data/processed/spatial_vars.rds")
    spatial_vars <- spatial_vars %>%
      select(-any_of(c("dist_good_school_km", "dist_std_school_km"))) %>%
      left_join(new_cols, by = "wijk_code")
  } else {
    spatial_vars <- new_cols
  }

  saveRDS(spatial_vars, "data/processed/spatial_vars.rds")
  cat("spatial_vars columns:", ncol(spatial_vars), "\n")
  message("Spatial variables updated with school quality distances.")
}
```
The quality-split distances make intuitive sense. Good schools have a median of ~2.15 km and mean of ~2.79 km — substantially further than standard schools (median ~0.82 km, mean ~1.20 km). This ratio of roughly 2.6x is entirely expected: there are far fewer good schools (~1,207 vs ~4,791 standard schools), so on average a wijk has to look further to find one. The maximum distance of ~26 km for good schools reflects a remote rural wijk with no high-performing school nearby — a meaningful real-world finding that illustrates the geographic concentration of school quality in the Netherlands. All spatial variables are appended to `spatial_vars.rds` for merging with the CBS data in the next section.

---

# Merge and Exploratory Data Analysis

## Merging CBS and Spatial Data

At this point we have two separate data objects: the CBS panel with all demographic, housing, and car ownership variables, and `spatial_vars` with the school distance and density measures computed from DUO coordinates. We join them on `wijk_code` using a left join — keeping all CBS districts and attaching spatial variables where available. If `spatial_vars.rds` is missing (e.g. the spatial chunks were skipped), the script substitutes NA columns so the rest of the pipeline doesn't break.

```{r merge}
cbs <- readRDS("data/processed/cbs_clean.rds")

if (file.exists("data/processed/spatial_vars.rds")) {
  sp_vars <- readRDS("data/processed/spatial_vars.rds")
  df <- cbs %>% left_join(sp_vars, by = "wijk_code")
  message("Spatial distance matched: ",
          sum(!is.na(df$dist_school_centroid_km)), " districts")
} else {
  message("Spatial vars not found — using CBS proximity measures only (dist_primary_school).")
  df <- cbs %>%
    mutate(dist_school_centroid_km = NA_real_,
           n_schools_1km           = NA_integer_,
           n_schools_1km           = NA_integer_)
}

message("Merged dataset: ", nrow(df), " rows x ", ncol(df), " columns")
```
The merge produces ~3,232 rows and ~31 columns. The drop from 3,352 to 3,232 happened in the `cbs-clean` chunk earlier — CBS suppresses WOZ values for very small districts. All remaining districts found a spatial match, confirming the `wijk_code` keys are consistent between the CBS and DUO/spatial datasets.

## Choosing the Proximity Variable

We now have two school distance measures: `dist_primary_school` (CBS-reported average distance from all residential addresses to the nearest school) and `dist_school_centroid_km` (our own centroid-based measure). The CBS measure is preferred as the main variable because it better reflects the actual residential experience of households. The centroid measure serves as a sensitivity check (Appendix).

`prox_main` is created as the CBS distance, falling back to the centroid measure only if the CBS value is missing for a given district (`coalesce()`). `log_prox` is a log-transformed version available for robustness checks. `school_density_3km` simply renames the CBS-provided `n_schools_3km` for clarity.

```{r proximity-var}
df <- df %>%
  mutate(
    prox_main          = coalesce(dist_primary_school, dist_school_centroid_km), # if dist_primary_school NA, it takes dist_school_centroid_km value
    log_prox           = log(prox_main + 0.01), # natural log, 0.01 is added to avoid negative infinity (distance = 0)
    school_density_3km = n_schools_3km   # CBS reports schools within 3 km in 85618NED (renames)
  )
```

## Final Sample Restrictions

Before running any models, we apply five filters to form the regression sample. These are applied once here and the cleaned dataset is saved to disk — all subsequent analyses load from `analysis_data.rds` rather than re-applying the filters.

```{r sample-filter}
n_before <- nrow(df)

df <- df %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(log_woz),
    !is.na(prox_main),
    !is.na(pct_single_hh),
    !is.na(income_avg_k),
    pop_total > 500
  )

message("Final sample: ", nrow(df), " districts (dropped ", n_before - nrow(df), ")")

# Flag outlier districts (outside 1%–99% of WOZ distribution)
p01 <- quantile(df$log_woz, 0.01)
p99 <- quantile(df$log_woz, 0.99)
df  <- df %>% mutate(woz_outlier = log_woz < p01 | log_woz > p99)

# Add singles tercile for EDA plots
df <- df %>%
  mutate(
    singles_tercile = case_when(
      pct_single_hh <= quantile(pct_single_hh, 1/3, na.rm = TRUE) ~ "Low singles (family-rich)",
      pct_single_hh <= quantile(pct_single_hh, 2/3, na.rm = TRUE) ~ "Medium singles",
      TRUE                                                          ~ "High singles"
    ),
    singles_tercile = factor(singles_tercile,
                             levels = c("Low singles (family-rich)",
                                        "Medium singles", "High singles"))
  )

saveRDS(df, "data/processed/analysis_data.rds")
```

The message confirms how many districts were dropped and how many remain in the final sample. The five filters remove districts with missing WOZ, proximity, singles share, or income data (CBS suppresses values for very small or recently created areas), and exclude districts with fewer than 500 residents, where WOZ averages are based on too few transactions to be reliable. The 500-resident threshold is a standard choice in the CBS literature. The outlier flag (`woz_outlier`) marks districts outside the 1st–99th percentile of the log WOZ distribution — these are retained in the data but can be excluded in sensitivity checks. The `singles_tercile` variable splits districts into three equal-sized groups by singles share; it is used only for the exploratory heterogeneity plot (Figure 4) and does not enter any regression.

---

## Leefbaarometer: Neighbourhood Quality Control

A key threat to identification in the cross-sectional model is that districts with good schools may also be generally nicer neighbourhoods — better maintained, safer, more cohesive — and those characteristics independently raise house prices. Without controlling for overall neighbourhood quality, the school proximity coefficient would absorb some of this neighbourhood quality premium, biasing our estimates.

The Leefbaarometer (published by the Ministry of the Interior) addresses this directly. It is a composite liveability index covering five dimensions: housing stock quality, physical environment, local services and amenities, social cohesion, and safety/nuisance. It is published every two years for all Dutch wijken. We use the 2022 edition for the 2023 cross-section, and year-matched editions for the panel (2018→2018, 2019→2018, 2020→2020, 2021→2020, 2022→2022, 2023→2022).

Unlike the CBS data, the Leefbaarometer is not available via API — it must be downloaded manually from the Ministry's website and placed in `data/raw/`. The chunk searches for the file automatically and stops with a clear error message if it is not found.

## Downloading Leefbaarometer Data

```{r lbm-download, cache=TRUE}
# ── Locate the manually downloaded Leefbaarometer wijk scores CSV ────────────
# Expected location: data/raw/leefbaarometer_wijken.csv
# If not found, also search data/raw/ for any CSV with "wijken" or "wijk" in the name
lbm_csv <- "data/raw/leefbaarometer_wijken.csv"

if (!file.exists(lbm_csv)) {
  candidates <- list.files("data/raw", pattern = "wijk", ignore.case = TRUE,
                           full.names = TRUE)
  candidates <- candidates[grepl("\\.csv$", candidates, ignore.case = TRUE)]
  if (length(candidates) > 0) {
    lbm_csv <- candidates[1]
    cat("Found Leefbaarometer file at:", lbm_csv, "\n")
  } else {
    stop("Leefbaarometer wijk CSV not found in data/raw/.\n",
         "Please copy 'Leefbaarometer-scores wijken 2002-2022.csv' from the\n",
         "downloaded zip into data/raw/ and rename it 'leefbaarometer_wijken.csv'.")
  }
}

lbm_raw <- read.csv(lbm_csv, stringsAsFactors = FALSE, check.names = FALSE)
cat("Leefbaarometer:", nrow(lbm_raw), "rows x", ncol(lbm_raw), "cols\n")
cat("Columns:", paste(names(lbm_raw), collapse = ", "), "\n")
jaar_col <- grep("^jaar$|^year$", names(lbm_raw), ignore.case = TRUE, value = TRUE)[1]
cat("Years available:", paste(sort(unique(lbm_raw[[jaar_col]])), collapse = ", "), "\n")
cat("\nFirst 5 rows:\n")
print(head(lbm_raw[, c("wk_code", jaar_col, "lbm")], 5))
```

## Standardising and Merging

```{r lbm-merge}
# ── Identify key columns ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Leefbaarometer uses Dutch column names; detect them robustly
code_col  <- grep("wk_code|wijkcode|code", names(lbm_raw), ignore.case = TRUE, value = TRUE)[1]
year_col  <- grep("^jaar$|^year$", names(lbm_raw), ignore.case = TRUE, value = TRUE)[1]
score_col <- grep("^lbm$|leefbaar|score", names(lbm_raw), ignore.case = TRUE, value = TRUE)[1]

cat("Using columns — code:", code_col, "| year:", year_col, "| score:", score_col, "\n")

# ── Year mapping: panel year → closest prior Leefbaarometer measurement ─────
year_map <- c(
  "2018" = 2018, "2019" = 2018,
  "2020" = 2020, "2021" = 2020,
  "2022" = 2022, "2023" = 2022
)

# ── Build clean Leefbaarometer table ────────────────────────────────────────
lbm_clean <- lbm_raw %>%
  rename(wijk_code  = all_of(code_col),
         lbm_year   = all_of(year_col),
         lbm_score  = all_of(score_col)) %>%
  filter(lbm_year %in% c(2018, 2020, 2022)) %>%
  mutate(wijk_code = str_trim(as.character(wijk_code)),
         lbm_score = as.numeric(lbm_score)) %>%
  select(wijk_code, lbm_year, lbm_score)

cat("Leefbaarometer clean:", nrow(lbm_clean), "rows |",
    n_distinct(lbm_clean$wijk_code), "unique wijken\n")

# ── Merge onto 2023 cross-section (use 2022 score) ──────────────────────────
lbm_2022 <- lbm_clean %>% filter(lbm_year == 2022) %>% select(wijk_code, lbm_score)

df <- df %>%
  select(-any_of("lbm_score")) %>%        # drop if re-running chunk
  left_join(lbm_2022, by = "wijk_code")

cat("Cross-section matched:", sum(!is.na(df$lbm_score)), "/", nrow(df), "\n")

# ── Merge onto panel (use year-matched score) ────────────────────────────────
# Note: panel_df is created in twfe-prep; this block is skipped if not yet in memory
if (exists("panel_df")) {
  panel_df <- panel_df %>%
    select(-any_of(c("lbm_score", "lbm_year"))) %>%
    mutate(lbm_year = as.integer(year_map[as.character(year)])) %>%
    left_join(lbm_clean, by = c("wijk_code", "lbm_year")) %>%
    select(-lbm_year)
  cat("Panel matched:", sum(!is.na(panel_df$lbm_score)), "/", nrow(panel_df), "\n")
} else {
  message("panel_df not yet in memory — lbm join will be applied in twfe-prep.")
}
```
The Leefbaarometer clean table has ~9,910 rows (3 years × ~3,303 wijken), matching the expected coverage. The cross-section match rate is ~95.3% (2,678/2,809) and the panel rate is ~95.5% (15,565/16,298) — the ~5% unmatched are very small or recently created wijken not covered by the Leefbaarometer. These will be dropped by listwise deletion in the regression sample, which is acceptable.

The year mapping deserves a brief note: the Leefbaarometer is published every two years, so panel years without a direct match (2019, 2021, 2023) use the most recent prior edition. This means the liveability score is a lagged measure for odd years — a minor limitation acknowledged in the thesis.

## Summary Statistics

The summary statistics table covers all variables that appear in the regression models or are discussed in the descriptive analysis. This table will be included in the thesis — it gives the reader a sense of the data before any modelling, and allows the reader to assess whether the sample is representative of the Netherlands as a whole.

**Data exploration table**

```{r summary-stats}
model_vars <- c(
  "log_woz", "woz_avg_k",
  "prox_main", "dist_school_centroid_km", "n_schools_3km",
  "pct_single_hh", "pct_hh_with_children", "pct_hh_no_children",  # pct_hh_with_children kept for context; not used as regressor
  "delta_singles_lag1",                       # lagged Δ singles — instrument
  "income_avg_k", "pct_employed",
  "pop_density_km2", "pct_age_0_14",          # pct_owner_occupied excluded: r = -0.85 with pct_single_hh
  "pct_owner_occupied",                       # shown in table for descriptive context only
  "cars_per_hh"                               # car ownership per household — mobility control
)

sumstats <- df %>%
  select(all_of(intersect(model_vars, names(df)))) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable") %>%
  group_by(variable) %>%
  summarise(
    N      = sum(!is.na(value)),
    Mean   = round(mean(value,              na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    SD     = round(sd(value,               na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    Median = round(median(value,            na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    Min    = round(min(value,              na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    Max    = round(max(value,              na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

write.csv(sumstats, "output/tables/summary_stats.csv", row.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(sumstats, caption = "Descriptive statistics — wijk level")
```

**Paper-ready version**. It includes the dependent variable + every variable that appears in at least one main regression model.

```{r summary-stats-paper-ready}

# This replaces the manual pivot-longer approach with a publication-ready table.
# Only the variables that appear in regression models (or as context) are included.
library(kableExtra)

ds_vars <- df %>%
  select(
    `Log WOZ value`                  = log_woz,
    `Avg. WOZ value (k€)`            = woz_avg_k,

    `ΔSingles share, lag 1 (%)`      = delta_singles_lag1,
    `Cars per household`             = cars_per_hh,

    `Employment rate (%)`            = pct_employed,
    `Population density (per km²)`   = pop_density_km2,

  )

tbl_desc <- datasummary_skim(

  histogram = FALSE
) |>
  kable_styling(

tbl_desc |> save_kable("output/tables/desc_stats.html", self_contained = TRUE)
webshot2::webshot("output/tables/desc_stats.html",
```
