All values are plausible and internally consistent:

- `log_woz` mean 12.8 → exp(12.8) ≈ €362k, consistent with `woz_avg_k` mean of €382k. The small difference reflects the inequality effect of log-transforming a right-skewed variable.
- `pct_owner_occupied` mean ~66% — high homeownership typical for the Netherlands.
- `income_avg_k` mean ~42k, median ~40k — plausible Dutch household income levels.
- The three household-composition variables sum to ~100%: `pct_single_hh` (~34%) + `pct_hh_no_children` (~31%) + `pct_hh_with_children` (~34%) = ~100%, confirming CBS counts `hh_no_children` as multi-person households *without* children (not including singles).
- `cars_per_hh` N=2,791 (slightly fewer than other variables) — consistent with the 133 suppressed values seen in the missingness check, with most of the suppressed districts already excluded by the pop > 500 filter.
- `delta_singles_lag1` N≈2,556 — 253 districts in the 2023 cross-section lack sufficient panel history for the lag calculation. These receive NA and are excluded from panel models but not cross-sectional ones.

Note: `pct_hh_with_children` is shown for descriptive context but is not used in any regression — it is replaced by `pct_age_0_14` to avoid the high collinearity with `pct_single_hh` (r = −0.85).

## Figure 1: Key Variable Distributions

Figure 1 combines the distributions of the dependent variable (panel A) and the key moderating variable (panel B) into a single two-panel figure. Together they justify both the log transformation of WOZ values and the plausibility of identifying a tipping point within the singles share distribution.

```{r fig-distributions, fig.cap="(A) WOZ value distribution across Dutch districts; (B) Single-person household share distribution.", fig.width=11, fig.height=4.5}
p_woz <- ggplot(df, aes(x = woz_avg_k)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = "#2E5D9E", colour = "white", alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma_format(suffix = "k€")) +
  labs(
    title    = "(A) Average WOZ value by district",
    subtitle = "CBS Kerncijfers Wijken en Buurten, Netherlands",
    x        = "Average WOZ value (thousands of euros)",
    y        = "Number of districts"
  )

p_singles <- ggplot(df, aes(x = pct_single_hh)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "#E07B39", colour = "white", alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = median(df$pct_single_hh, na.rm = TRUE),
             linetype = "dashed", colour = "black", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text",
           x     = median(df$pct_single_hh, na.rm = TRUE) + 2,
           y     = Inf, vjust = 2,
           label = paste0("Median: ",
                          round(median(df$pct_single_hh, na.rm = TRUE), 1), "%"),
           size  = 3.5) +
  labs(
    title    = "(B) Single-person household share",
    subtitle = "Key moderating variable — higher = more singles-dominant districts",
    x        = "Share of single-person households (%)",
    y        = "Number of districts"
  )

p_woz + p_singles
```

**Panel A**: The WOZ distribution is right-skewed with a peak around €300–400k and a long upper tail reaching ~€1.8M (premium Amsterdam canal districts and coastal areas). The mean (~€382k) exceeds the median (~€363k), confirming the skew. This is exactly why `log_woz` is the correct outcome variable — the log transformation compresses the right tail, producing a more symmetric distribution and yielding coefficients directly interpretable as percentage changes in house values.

**Panel B**: The singles share distribution is right-skewed with a median of ~31% and a long tail reaching ~98% (inner-city Amsterdam and student-dominated districts). Most wijken cluster between 25–40%, with a substantial number above 50% — this tail is precisely the range where the tipping point hypothesis predicts a sign reversal. The existence of enough high-singles districts gives the models statistical power to identify the conditional tipping point found in Model H.

## Figure 2:  Motivating Evidence

Figure 2 presents two exploratory plots: the first shows the raw bivariate relationship between school proximity and WOZ values, and the second shows how that relationship differs across demographic groups — the visual preview of the tipping point hypothesis.

```{r fig-motivating, fig.cap=c("Raw proximity–WOZ relationship.", "Proximity effect by single-person household share tercile."), fig.width=9, fig.height=5.5}
p_prox <- ggplot(df, aes(x = prox_main, y = log_woz)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2, size = 0.8, colour = "#1F3864") +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", colour = "#E07B39", se = TRUE, linewidth = 1.1) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 5)) +
  labs(
    title    = "School proximity and log WOZ values",
    subtitle = "LOESS fit with 95% CI | x-axis clipped at 5km",
    x        = "Distance to nearest primary school (km)",
    y        = "Log average WOZ value"
  )

p_het <- ggplot(df, aes(x = prox_main, y = log_woz, colour = singles_tercile)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 4)) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c("#1E7B4B", "#2E5D9E", "#C0392B"),
    name   = "Single-person\nhousehold share"
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Proximity effect by single-HH share tercile",
    subtitle = "If H2 & H3 hold: green slope ↓ (premium), red slope ↑ (discount)",
    x        = "Distance to nearest primary school (km)",
    y        = "Log average WOZ value"
  )

print(p_prox)
print(p_het)
```
**Figure 2a:** The LOESS curve shows a non-monotonic pattern: WOZ values increase with distance from 0 to ~2km, then gradually decline. There is no simple "closer = more valuable" relationship in the aggregate. This is not a problem — it is actually the central motivation for the research question. The likely explanation is urban-suburban confounding: urban districts have many schools nearby *and* lower WOZ (smaller apartments, more singles), while suburban districts have fewer schools *and* higher WOZ (larger family homes). These opposite forces cancel out in the raw data, masking the true proximity effect.

Two technical features of the plot are worth noting. The vertical striping of points occurs because CBS rounds `dist_primary_school` to one decimal place — this is a measurement artifact and harmless. The widening confidence interval beyond 2km reflects the thinning of observations in that range.

This figure motivates the regression directly: the aggregate relationship is confounded by spatial sorting, and municipality fixed effects are needed to isolate the within-gemeente proximity effect from the between-city variation.

**Figure 2b:** All three lines have positive slopes — WOZ increases with distance in every tercile, which is the opposite of what H2 predicts for the family-rich (green) group. This is driven by the same urban-suburban confounding: family-rich districts tend to be suburban with large expensive houses *and* schools far away, while high-singles districts are urban with cheaper, denser housing *and* schools nearby. The slopes reflect this spatial sorting, not a genuine proximity effect.

Two observations are worth noting for the thesis. First, the three lines are roughly parallel — the slopes are similar across groups — meaning the heterogeneity by demographic composition is not visible in unconditional data. This directly motivates the controlled regression: only after absorbing municipality fixed effects and socioeconomic controls can we isolate the within-gemeente proximity effect separately for each demographic group. Second, the red (high-singles) line sits consistently below the other two at every distance, confirming that higher singles share is associated with lower WOZ regardless of proximity — supporting the additional finding that `pct_single_hh` has an independent negative effect on house values.

## Correlation Matrix

Before running regressions, it is useful to examine pairwise correlations to anticipate potential multicollinearity and check that relationships go in the expected direction. Note that these are raw cross-sectional correlations, which include both within- and between-municipality variation. They will be inflated by spatial sorting — the within-gemeente correlations in the next subsection are the more relevant diagnostic for the regression.

```{r correlation}
corr_vars <- c("log_woz", "prox_main", "pct_single_hh",
               "pct_hh_with_children", "pct_owner_occupied",
               "income_avg_k", "pct_employed", "pop_density_km2", "pct_age_0_14",
               "cars_per_hh", "lbm_score")

corr_data   <- df %>% select(all_of(intersect(corr_vars, names(df)))) %>% drop_na()
corr_matrix <- round(cor(corr_data), 2)

knitr::kable(as.data.frame(corr_matrix), caption = "Pairwise correlation matrix")
write.csv(as.data.frame(corr_matrix), "output/tables/correlation_matrix.csv")
```

The raw correlations reveal the expected patterns. `lbm_score` is the strongest correlate of WOZ (r = 0.78 within-gemeente, see below), confirming neighbourhood quality is a crucial control. `income_avg_k` is also strongly positive (r = 0.70). `pct_single_hh` is negatively associated with WOZ (r = −0.44) and strongly negatively correlated with `cars_per_hh` (r = −0.80) — urban singles own fewer cars. The high correlations between `pct_single_hh`, `pct_owner_occupied`, and `cars_per_hh` (all around ±0.82–0.85) reflect urban-suburban sorting that municipality fixed effects will largely absorb. The strong correlation of `pct_owner_occupied` with the key regressors motivates running Models A and B in parallel — Model A excludes `pct_owner_occupied` while Model B includes it — to assess whether adding this variable materially inflates standard errors through multicollinearity or whether the precision gain from controlling for tenure composition outweighs the cost. Same in panel specification with Models C and D.

## Within-Municipality Correlation Matrix

The cross-sectional correlations above are inflated by spatial sorting: cities simultaneously have high singles shares, low owner-occupation, and are denser. Municipality fixed effects remove this between-group variation. The table below shows correlations computed on **within-gemeente demeaned variables** — the variation actually used by the fixed-effects estimator.

```{r correlation-within}
corr_vars_model <- c("log_woz", "prox_main", "pct_single_hh",
                     "pct_owner_occupied", "income_avg_k",
                     "pct_employed", "pop_density_km2", "pct_age_0_14",
                     "cars_per_hh", "lbm_score")

within_corr <- df %>%
  select(gemeente_code, all_of(intersect(corr_vars_model, names(df)))) %>%
  drop_na() %>%
  group_by(gemeente_code) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ . - mean(.))) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(-gemeente_code)

within_matrix <- round(cor(within_corr), 2)

knitr::kable(as.data.frame(within_matrix),
             caption = "Within-municipality correlation matrix (gemeente-demeaned variables)")
write.csv(as.data.frame(within_matrix),
          "output/tables/correlation_within_gemeente.csv")
```

Municipality fixed effects remove the between-city variation that was inflating the raw correlations. Three within-gemeente findings are most relevant for model specification:

**`pct_single_hh` vs `pct_owner_occupied` (r = −0.79 within-gemeente):** this dropped from −0.83 in the raw data, confirming that municipality FEs absorb a meaningful share of the collinearity. The within-gemeente correlation is high but below the informal 0.8 threshold, so `pct_owner_occupied` can be retained in the model. We estimate both versions (A without, B with) and compare standard errors to verify.

**`cars_per_hh` vs `pct_single_hh` (r = −0.74 within-gemeente):** also high. This is important for Models H and J — the two moderators are substantially correlated within municipalities, meaning their interaction terms cannot be fully separated. The conditional tipping point in Section 10 must therefore be interpreted as reflecting the *joint* moderating role of demographics and car ownership.

**`lbm_score` vs `log_woz` (r = +0.78 within-gemeente):** the Leefbaarometer is the single strongest predictor of WOZ within municipalities. Its correlations with the control variables are all moderate (income 0.54, owner-occupied 0.57, cars 0.40, singles −0.34), confirming it adds explanatory power without creating severe multicollinearity.

Based on these diagnostics, the preferred baseline specification includes the Leefbaarometer score, with municipality fixed effects and standard errors clustered at the gemeente level.

---

# Regression Analysis

The regression analysis proceeds in four steps. First, a **baseline hedonic model** (Model 0) establishes the average proximity effect within municipalities. Second, **interaction models** (A and B) test whether the singles share moderates that effect — the core test of H2 and H3. Third, a **panel TWFE model** (C and D) adds district and year fixed effects to exploit within-district variation over time and remove time-invariant district-level confounders. Fourth, **extensions** (E–J) investigate school quality heterogeneity and car ownership as a mobility moderator.

All models use `fixest::feols()`, which is purpose-built for models with high-dimensional fixed effects and provides fast computation with clustered standard errors.

```{r reg-setup}
library(fixest)
```

## Baseline Hedonic Model

Model 0 is the simplest hedonic specification: log WOZ regressed on school proximity and socioeconomic controls, with municipality fixed effects. It answers the question: *on average, within a municipality, do districts closer to a primary school have higher or lower WOZ values?* Standard errors are clustered at the gemeente level to account for within-municipality correlation in house prices across wijken.

```{r m-baseline}
m0 <- feols(
  log_woz ~ prox_main + income_avg_k + pct_employed +
            pop_density_km2 + pct_age_0_14 + lbm_score | gemeente_code,
  data = df,
  vcov = ~gemeente_code
)
summary(m0)
```
The baseline model establishes the core finding: within municipalities, each additional kilometre of distance from the nearest school is associated with approximately **3.9% higher WOZ** (β = 0.039, p < 0.001). **H1 is rejected** — school proximity is a price discount, not a premium. The Leefbaarometer score is by far the dominant predictor (β = 1.200\*\*\*, meaning a 0.1-unit improvement in liveability → ~12% higher WOZ), confirming neighbourhood quality control was essential. Population density is negative (β = −0.000\*\*\*) — denser districts have lower WOZ within municipalities once liveability is absorbed. The share of children aged 0–14 is positive and significant (β = 0.008\*\*\*), consistent with child-rich districts being relatively expensive family neighbourhoods. Income (0.006\*\*\*) and employment (0.007\*\*\*) are both positive as expected. Adj. R² = 0.899.


## Interaction Models: Does Singles Share Moderate the Proximity Effect?

Models A and B extend the baseline by adding `pct_single_hh` and its interaction with `prox_main`. In the notation of the research proposal, β₃ is the key parameter: a positive β₃ (i.e. `prox_main:pct_single_hh` > 0) was expected under H2 — assuming H1 holds, β₃ > 0 makes the marginal effect of distance less negative (premium weakens) as singles share rises. Model B additionally includes `pct_owner_occupied`, whose inclusion is justified by the SE comparison below.

```{r m-interaction}
# Model A — interaction, no pct_owner_occupied
mA <- feols(
  log_woz ~ prox_main * pct_single_hh +
            income_avg_k + pct_employed + pop_density_km2 + pct_age_0_14 +
            lbm_score | gemeente_code,
  data = df,
  vcov = ~gemeente_code
)

# Model B — interaction, with pct_owner_occupied
mB <- feols(
  log_woz ~ prox_main * pct_single_hh +
            income_avg_k + pct_employed + pop_density_km2 + pct_age_0_14 +
            pct_owner_occupied + lbm_score | gemeente_code,
  data = df,
  vcov = ~gemeente_code
)
```

```{r m-controls-only-with-cars}
# Model B0 — distance + singles + cars as plain controls (no interactions)
mB0 <- feols(
  log_woz ~ prox_main + pct_single_hh + cars_per_hh +
            income_avg_k + pct_employed + pop_density_km2 + pct_age_0_14 +
            pct_owner_occupied + lbm_score | gemeente_code,
  data = df,
  vcov = ~gemeente_code
)

summary(mB0)
```


## Comparing Standard Errors: Model A vs. Model B

A common concern when adding a highly correlated variable (`pct_owner_occupied`, within-gemeente r = −0.79 with `pct_single_hh`) is that standard errors on the key terms inflate, reducing precision. We compare SEs across the two models and apply a 20% inflation threshold — if SE inflation on the interaction term exceeds 20%, Model A is preferred; otherwise Model B is chosen.

```{r se-comparison}
key_terms <- c("prox_main", "pct_single_hh", "prox_main:pct_single_hh")

se_compare <- data.frame(
  Term      = key_terms,
  SE_ModelA = se(mA)[key_terms],
  SE_ModelB = se(mB)[key_terms]
) %>%
  mutate(
    Inflation_pct = round(100 * (SE_ModelB / SE_ModelA - 1), 1)
  )

print(se_compare)
cat("\nRule of thumb: prefer Model B if SE inflation on interaction term < 20%\n")

# Choose preferred model for downstream plots
m_preferred <- if (se_compare$Inflation_pct[3] < 20) mB else mA
cat("Preferred model:", if (identical(m_preferred, mB)) "Model B" else "Model A", "\n")
```
All three key terms have SE changes well within the 20% threshold — `prox_main` and the interaction term actually tighten (negative inflation), and `pct_single_hh` inflates by only ~11%. Adding `pct_owner_occupied` improves rather than harms precision, confirming Model B as the preferred cross-sectional specification.

## Regression Table

```{r model-table}
tbl_args <- list( # store all shared arguments in a list
  models    = list("(0) Baseline" = m0, "(B0) Controls" = mB0, "(A) Interaction" = mA, "(B) + Owner-occ." = mB),
  stars     = c("*" = 0.05, "**" = 0.01, "***" = 0.001),
  coef_map  = c(
    "prox_main"               = "Distance to school (km)",
    "pct_single_hh"           = "Single-HH share (%)",
    "cars_per_hh"             = "Cars per household",
    "prox_main:pct_single_hh" = "Distance × Single-HH share",
    "income_avg_k"            = "Avg. household income (k€)",
    "pct_employed"            = "Employment rate (%)",
    "pop_density_km2"         = "Population density (per km²)",
    "pct_age_0_14"            = "Share aged 0–14 (%)",
    "pct_owner_occupied"      = "Owner-occupied (%)",
    "lbm_score"               = "Liveability score (Leefbaarometer)"
  ),
  gof_map   = c("nobs", "r.squared", "adj.r.squared"),
  title     = "Hedonic regression: school proximity and log WOZ values",
  notes     = "Municipality (gemeente) fixed effects in all models. Standard errors clustered at gemeente level."
)

# Display inline
do.call(modelsummary, tbl_args)

# Save to file
do.call(modelsummary, c(tbl_args, list(output = "output/tables/regression_table.html")))
```

**Interpretation**

*Model 0 — Baseline.* Each additional kilometre from the nearest school is associated with 3.9% higher WOZ within municipalities (β ≈ 0.039, p < 0.01). **H1 is rejected**: school proximity is on average a price discount, not a premium. This is the central finding of the cross-sectional analysis.

*Models A and B — Interaction.* Adding the singles interaction changes the interpretation of the distance coefficient: it now represents the proximity effect only at singles share = 0, which is outside the observed data range. The coefficient rises to 0.049\*\* — not because the discount increased, but because the meaning of the coefficient changed. The meaningful quantity is the full marginal effect across the observed range (see marginal effects plot). `Single-HH share` is negative and significant in both models (β = −0.005\*\*\* in A, −0.003\*\* in B) — within municipalities, higher singles share independently lowers WOZ. The `Distance × Single-HH share` interaction is −0.000 in both models — **H2 and H3 are not supported** in this specification. Model B adds `owner-occupied` (β = 0.002\*\*\*), which tightens rather than inflates standard errors. Note that `share aged 0–14` loses significance in Model A (0.002) and is only marginally significant in B (0.003\*), reflecting collinearity with the singles share variable. Adj. R² rises from 0.899 (Model 0) to 0.907 (A) and 0.909 (B).

## Marginal Effects Plot

Even though the interaction term is not statistically significant in Models A/B, it is informative to visualise the full marginal effect of distance across the range of singles share. The marginal effect is: ∂log_woz/∂prox_main = β₁ + β₃ × pct_single_hh. We compute this at 200 equally spaced values of `pct_single_hh` from the observed minimum to maximum, with 95% confidence intervals obtained via the delta method (Brambor et al., 2006).

```{r marginal-effects, fig.cap="Marginal effect of a 1 km increase in distance to school on log WOZ, by singles share. Shaded band: 95% CI (gemeente-clustered)."}
b1 <- coef(m_preferred)["prox_main"]
b3 <- coef(m_preferred)["prox_main:pct_single_hh"]

singles_seq <- seq(
  min(df$pct_single_hh, na.rm = TRUE),
  max(df$pct_single_hh, na.rm = TRUE),
  length.out = 200
)

# Delta-method SE: Var(β1 + β3*x) = Var(β1) + x²·Var(β3) + 2x·Cov(β1,β3)
v     <- vcov(m_preferred)[c("prox_main", "prox_main:pct_single_hh"),
                            c("prox_main", "prox_main:pct_single_hh")]
me    <- b1 + b3 * singles_seq
se_me <- sqrt(v[1,1] + singles_seq^2 * v[2,2] + 2 * singles_seq * v[1,2])

me_df <- tibble(
  singles = singles_seq,
  me      = me,
  lower   = me - 1.96 * se_me,
  upper   = me + 1.96 * se_me
)

ggplot(me_df, aes(x = singles, y = me)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), fill = "grey80", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_line(colour = "#2E5D9E", linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = max(singles_seq) * 0.85, y = 0.001,
           label = "Zero effect", colour = "grey40", size = 3.2, vjust = -0.5) +
  labs(
    title    = "Marginal effect of school distance on log WOZ",
    subtitle = "By single-person household share | 95% CI from delta method",
    x        = "Single-person household share (%)",
    y        = "ME of distance (km) on log WOZ"
  )

ggsave("output/figures/marginal_effects.png", width = 9, height = 5.5, dpi = 150)
```
The marginal effect declines as singles share rises, from ~0.047 at the low-singles end to ~0.015 at the high-singles tail. The blue line stays above zero throughout, but the lower bound of the 95% CI crosses zero around 75%+ singles share. The CI has a wedge/triangle shape, narrow on the left and widening dramatically to the right. This reflects the distribution of observations: most wijken cluster around 25–40% singles, where estimates are precise. Very few districts are above 75% singles, so uncertainty is large there and the interaction effect cannot be precisely identified. The declining slope is directionally consistent with H2 but statistically insignificant in this specification.

## Tipping Point

The tipping point is derived analytically from the condition ∂log_woz/∂prox_main = 0: pct_single_hh\* = −β₁/β₃. A 95% confidence interval is obtained via the delta method, using the gradient of the tipping point formula with respect to β₁ and β₃.

```{r tipping-point}
b1 <- coef(m_preferred)["prox_main"]
b3 <- coef(m_preferred)["prox_main:pct_single_hh"]
v  <- vcov(m_preferred)[c("prox_main", "prox_main:pct_single_hh"),
                         c("prox_main", "prox_main:pct_single_hh")]

tp <- -b1 / b3

# Gradient: ∂(-β1/β3)/∂β1 = -1/β3,  ∂(-β1/β3)/∂β3 = β1/β3²
grad  <- c(-1 / b3, b1 / b3^2)
tp_se <- as.numeric(sqrt(t(grad) %*% v %*% grad))
tp_ci <- tp + c(-1.96, 1.96) * tp_se

cat("Tipping point estimate:   ", round(tp, 1), "% single-person households\n")
cat("95% CI:                  [", round(tp_ci[1], 1), ",", round(tp_ci[2], 1), "]\n")
cat("Sample median singles:    ", round(median(df$pct_single_hh, na.rm = TRUE), 1), "%\n")
cat("Sample 75th percentile:   ", round(quantile(df$pct_single_hh, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE), 1), "%\n")
cat("Tipping point exists:     ", !is.na(tp) && b1 * b3 < 0, "\n")
```


From Model B, β₁ (distance) is positive (+0.049) and β₃ (interaction) is slightly negative, so they have **opposite signs** — `Tipping point exists: TRUE`. Mathematically, a tipping point exists at **140.6%** singles share. However, this is far outside the feasible 0–100% range and therefore has no practical meaning — no Dutch district comes close to that demographic composition.

The 95% CI of [−222, +504] is enormous because β₃ is extremely close to zero: dividing by a near-zero number amplifies uncertainty massively, and the CI spans both sides of zero and extends far beyond the feasible range in both directions.

**The honest conclusion**: while the formula yields a mathematical solution, the tipping point is not identified within the observable data. School proximity is a consistent price discount across the full range of single-person household shares observed in the Netherlands. H3 is not supported in this specification. This motivates both the panel model — which uses stricter within-district identification — and the car ownership extension, where the conditional tipping point is identified at a realistic value (61%).

## Panel Two-Way Fixed Effects Model

The cross-sectional models absorb municipality-level unobservables but cannot rule out time-invariant *district*-level confounders. For example, a wijk that has always had many schools because it was built near a school, and also always had lower WOZ for unrelated reasons. The panel TWFE model addresses this by adding district fixed effects (αᵢ), which absorb all time-invariant characteristics of each wijk, and year fixed effects (γₜ), which absorb common annual shocks to the Dutch housing market (e.g. interest rate changes, national policy shifts). The identifying variation is purely within-district over time, changes in `dist_primary_school` and `pct_single_hh` within the same wijk between 2018 and 2023.

```{r twfe-prep}
panel_df <- readRDS("data/processed/cbs_panel.rds") %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(log_woz),
    !is.na(dist_primary_school),
    !is.na(pct_single_hh),
    !is.na(income_avg_k),
    pop_total > 500
  )

# ── Re-join Leefbaarometer scores (year-matched) ────────────────────────────
year_map <- c("2018" = 2018, "2019" = 2018, "2020" = 2020,
              "2021" = 2020, "2022" = 2022, "2023" = 2022)

lbm_raw   <- read.csv("data/raw/leefbaarometer_wijken.csv",
                       stringsAsFactors = FALSE, check.names = FALSE)
lbm_clean <- lbm_raw[lbm_raw$jaar %in% c(2018, 2020, 2022),
                      c("wk_code", "jaar", "lbm")]
names(lbm_clean) <- c("wijk_code", "lbm_year", "lbm_score")

panel_df <- panel_df %>%
  select(-any_of(c("lbm_score", "lbm_year"))) %>%
  mutate(lbm_year = as.integer(year_map[as.character(year)])) %>%
  left_join(lbm_clean, by = c("wijk_code", "lbm_year")) %>%
  select(-lbm_year)

cat("Panel observations:", nrow(panel_df), "\n")
cat("Districts:         ", n_distinct(panel_df$wijk_code), "\n")
cat("Years:             ", paste(sort(unique(panel_df$year)), collapse = ", "), "\n")
cat("lbm_score matched:", sum(!is.na(panel_df$lbm_score)), "/", nrow(panel_df), "\n")
cat("delta_singles_lag1 available:", sum(!is.na(panel_df$delta_singles_lag1)), "\n")
```

The panel covers 2018–2023 (6 years) rather than the full 2016–2023 range because CBS did not include `dist_primary_school` in the 2016 and 2017 editions, those years are dropped by the `!is.na(dist_primary_school)` filter. Six years is still a solid panel for identifying within-district variation. The `delta_singles_lag1` coverage of ~91% is acceptable, the remaining 9% are districts without panel history back to 2016/2017. The Leefbaarometer match rate of ~95.5% is consistent with the cross-section. These figures should be reported in a data appendix or footnote in the thesis.

```{r twfe-model}
# TWFE: district FE (wijk_code) + year FE
# Uses CBS-provided dist_primary_school, which varies by year as schools open/close
# delta_singles_lag1 controls for pre-period demographic momentum

# Model C — without pct_owner_occupied
m_twfe <- feols(
  log_woz ~ dist_primary_school * pct_single_hh +
            income_avg_k + pct_employed + pop_density_km2 + pct_age_0_14 +
            delta_singles_lag1 + lbm_score | wijk_code + year,
  data = panel_df,
  vcov = ~wijk_code
)

# Model D — with pct_owner_occupied (consistent with cross-sectional Model B)
m_twfe_D <- feols(
  log_woz ~ dist_primary_school * pct_single_hh +
            income_avg_k + pct_employed + pop_density_km2 + pct_age_0_14 +
            delta_singles_lag1 + pct_owner_occupied + lbm_score | wijk_code + year,
  data = panel_df,
  vcov = ~wijk_code
)

# SE comparison for the panel models
key_terms_twfe <- c("dist_primary_school", "pct_single_hh",
                    "dist_primary_school:pct_single_hh")

se_compare_twfe <- data.frame(
  Term      = key_terms_twfe,
  SE_ModelC = se(m_twfe)[key_terms_twfe],
  SE_ModelD = se(m_twfe_D)[key_terms_twfe]
) %>%
  mutate(Inflation_pct = round(100 * (SE_ModelD / SE_ModelC - 1), 1))

print(se_compare_twfe)
cat("\nAdj. R² Model C:", round(r2(m_twfe,   type = "ar2"), 4), "\n")
cat("Adj. R² Model D:", round(r2(m_twfe_D, type = "ar2"), 4), "\n")
```

All three SEs decrease in Model D (−7.8%, −9.2%, −5.6%) and Adj. R² improves from 0.9844 to 0.9847. **Model D preferred again**, consistent with the cross-section. 

## Full Results Table

```{r twfe-table}
twfe_tbl_args <- list(
  models   = list("(B0) CS Controls" = mB0,
                  "(A) CS Interaction" = mA,
                  "(B) CS + Owner-occ." = mB,
                  "(C) Panel TWFE" = m_twfe,
                  "(D) Panel + Owner-occ." = m_twfe_D),
  stars    = c("*" = 0.05, "**" = 0.01, "***" = 0.001),
  coef_map = c(
    "prox_main"                         = "Distance to school (km)",
    "dist_primary_school"               = "Distance to school (km)",
    "pct_single_hh"                     = "Single-HH share (%)",
    "cars_per_hh"             = "Cars per household",
    "prox_main:pct_single_hh"           = "Distance × Single-HH share",
    "dist_primary_school:pct_single_hh" = "Distance × Single-HH share",
    "income_avg_k"                      = "Avg. household income (k€)",
    "pct_employed"                      = "Employment rate (%)",
    "pop_density_km2"                   = "Population density (per km²)",
    "pct_age_0_14"                      = "Share aged 0–14 (%)",
    "pct_owner_occupied"                = "Owner-occupied (%)",
    "delta_singles_lag1"                = "ΔSingles share (lag 1)",
    "lbm_score"                         = "Liveability score (Leefbaarometer)"
  ),
  gof_map  = c("nobs", "r.squared", "adj.r.squared"),
  title    = "School proximity and log WOZ: cross-sectional and panel estimates",
  notes    = "Models A–B: gemeente FE, clustered SEs at gemeente level (2023 cross-section). Model C: district + year FE, clustered SEs at district level (2018–2023 panel)."
)

# Display inline
do.call(modelsummary, twfe_tbl_args)

# Save to file
do.call(modelsummary, c(twfe_tbl_args, list(output = "output/tables/full_results_table.html")))
webshot2::webshot("output/tables/full_results_table.html", 
                  "output/tables/full_results_table.png",
                  zoom = 2)  # zoom = 2 for high resolution
```
The combined cross-section and panel table reveals four consistent findings across all specifications:

**H1 (proximity premium) — Rejected.** The distance coefficient is positive and significant in the cross-section (0.049\*\*) and positive but insignificant in the panel (0.046–0.048). School proximity is a price discount in every specification.

**H2/H3 (tipping point) — Not confirmed here.** The interaction `Distance × Single-HH share` is −0.000 or −0.001 in all four models — negative and near-zero, which is inconsistent with the positive β₃ predicted by H2 (the proximity premium was expected to weaken with more singles, implying β₃ > 0). The tipping point is only identified once car ownership is jointly modelled (Section 10).

**Singles share — robustly negative.** `Single-HH share` is negative and significant across all models (−0.003 to −0.005, p < 0.01). Higher singles share independently lowers WOZ within municipalities and over time within districts.

**Liveability score — dominant predictor.** In the cross-section (~1.1\*\*\*) and panel (~0.3\*\*\*), the Leefbaarometer score is the strongest predictor. The smaller panel coefficient reflects that district FEs absorb permanent liveability differences — the within-district coefficient captures the WOZ impact of liveability *changes* over time.

Panel observations drop to ~14,350 from ~14,903 due to Leefbaarometer missingness (3.7% loss) — modest and acceptable. Model D is the preferred panel specification.

## Extension I: School Quality Split (Gibbons & Machin)

Gibbons & Machin (2006) showed that only the top-performing schools generate a hedonic price premium. For all other schools, proximity is either neutral or a discount. To test whether this holds in the Dutch context, we replace the main distance variable with school-quality-specific distances: `dist_good_school_km` (distance to the nearest top-20% school) and `dist_std_school_km` (distance to the nearest standard school). If the G&M mechanism holds, the coefficient on `dist_good_school_km` should be smaller (or negative) compared to `dist_std_school_km`. Models E and F are otherwise identical to Model B.

```{r school-quality-models}
# ── Check whether quality distances are available in df ─────────────────────
has_quality <- all(c("dist_good_school_km", "dist_std_school_km") %in% names(df))

if (!has_quality) {
  message("School quality distances not yet in df — re-run merge chunk after school-quality-distances.")
} else {
  # Model E — good schools (top 20%)
  mE <- feols(
    log_woz ~ dist_good_school_km * pct_single_hh +
              income_avg_k + pct_employed + pop_density_km2 + pct_age_0_14 +
              pct_owner_occupied + lbm_score | gemeente_code,
    data = df, vcov = ~gemeente_code
  )

  # Model F — standard schools (bottom 80%)
  mF <- feols(
    log_woz ~ dist_std_school_km * pct_single_hh +
              income_avg_k + pct_employed + pop_density_km2 + pct_age_0_14 +
              pct_owner_occupied + lbm_score | gemeente_code,
    data = df, vcov = ~gemeente_code
  )

  quality_tbl_args <- list(
    models   = list("(E) Good schools (top 20%)" = mE,
                    "(F) Standard schools (bottom 80%)" = mF),
    stars    = c("*" = 0.05, "**" = 0.01, "***" = 0.001),
    coef_map = c(
      "dist_good_school_km"               = "Distance to school (km)",
      "dist_std_school_km"                = "Distance to school (km)",
      "pct_single_hh"                     = "Single-HH share (%)",
      "dist_good_school_km:pct_single_hh" = "Distance × Single-HH share",
      "dist_std_school_km:pct_single_hh"  = "Distance × Single-HH share",
      "income_avg_k"                      = "Avg. household income (k€)",
      "pct_employed"                      = "Employment rate (%)",
      "pop_density_km2"                   = "Population density (per km²)",
      "pct_age_0_14"                      = "Share aged 0–14 (%)",
      "pct_owner_occupied"                = "Owner-occupied (%)",
      "lbm_score"                         = "Liveability score (Leefbaarometer)"
    ),
    gof_map  = c("nobs", "r.squared", "adj.r.squared"),
    title    = "School quality split: good vs standard schools (Gibbons & Machin robustness)",
    notes    = "Good schools = top 20% by standardised doorstroomtoets score (DUO 2023-2024). Municipality FE, clustered SEs at gemeente level."
  )

  # Use fixest::etable() — avoids modelsummary/plyr round_any conflict
  etable(mE, mF,
         headers    = list("(E) Good schools (top 20%)" = 1,
                           "(F) Standard schools (bottom 80%)" = 1),
         signif.code = c("***" = 0.001, "**" = 0.01, "*" = 0.05),
         notes      = "Good schools = top 20% by standardised doorstroomtoets score (DUO 2023-2024). Municipality FE, clustered SEs at gemeente level.")

do.call(modelsummary, c(quality_tbl_args, list(output = "output/tables/ext1_quality_table.html")))

  # Key coefficient summary
  ct_E <- summary(mE)$coeftable
  ct_F <- summary(mF)$coeftable
  cat("\nGood school distance coef:",
      round(ct_E["dist_good_school_km", "Estimate"], 4),
      "(p =", round(ct_E["dist_good_school_km", "Pr(>|t|)"], 3), ")\n")
  cat("Standard school distance coef:",
      round(ct_F["dist_std_school_km", "Estimate"], 4),
      "(p =", round(ct_F["dist_std_school_km", "Pr(>|t|)"], 3), ")\n")
  cat("\nG&M prediction: good school coef NEGATIVE (premium), standard coef POSITIVE (discount)\n")
}
```
```{r}
webshot2::webshot("output/tables/ext1_quality_table.html",
                  "output/tables/ext1_quality_table.png",
                  zoom = 2)
```
Both distance coefficients are positive, neither school type generates an outright proximity premium at the wijk level. However, the magnitude difference is informative: good school distance (β ≈ 0.013, p < 0.01) is roughly half the standard school discount (β ≈ 0.024, p < 0.05). Proximity to a good school is penalised substantially less than proximity to a standard school, a finding directionally consistent with Gibbons & Machin even though an outright premium is not found.

The absence of a negative coefficient for good schools reflects the wijk-level aggregation: at the district level, the nuisance effects of school traffic and noise affect all nearby residents regardless of school quality, while the quality premium only benefits families who select the school. G&M found their premium at the level of individual property transactions, a finer spatial resolution. The quality-split result should be reported as a partial confirmation of the G&M mechanism, not a refutation: *"the proximity discount is approximately half as large for top-20% schools (β = 0.013) as for standard schools (β = 0.024), consistent with the direction of Gibbons & Machin (2006)."*

Note: a panel version of the quality split is not estimated because `dist_good_school_km` and `dist_std_school_km` are derived from a single 2023 DUO snapshot and do not vary over time, they would be absorbed by district fixed effects in a TWFE model.

---

## Extension II: Car Ownership as a Mobility Moderator

**Motivation**

The rejection of H1 raises a natural question: why is school proximity consistently a price discount rather than a premium? One candidate mechanism is car ownership. In the Netherlands, the open enrollment system (*vrije schoolkeuze*) means proximity to a school does not guarantee access, households can and do send children to any school regardless of distance. For households with a car, physical proximity to a school is therefore irrelevant as an access benefit, and the only remaining effect of having a school nearby is the externalities (noise, traffic, parking pressure). This predicts that the proximity discount should be weaker in high-car districts, households there care less about school distance in either direction.

We test this by adding `cars_per_hh` (passenger cars per household, from CBS Kerncijfers) first as a plain control variable (Model G) — does the proximity coefficient change once car ownership is absorbed? — and then as a moderator (Model H) — does car ownership significantly moderate the proximity effect?

This is an exploratory extension motivated by the empirical null result on H1, and should be framed as such in the thesis rather than as a pre-specified hypothesis.

```{r cars-models}
# ── Model G: cars_per_hh as additional control (based on preferred Model B) ──
mG <- feols(
  log_woz ~ prox_main * pct_single_hh +
            income_avg_k + pct_employed + pop_density_km2 + pct_age_0_14 +
            pct_owner_occupied + lbm_score + cars_per_hh | gemeente_code,
  data = df,
  vcov = ~gemeente_code
)

# ── Model H: cars_per_hh as moderator of proximity effect ────────────────────
mH <- feols(
  log_woz ~ prox_main * pct_single_hh + prox_main * cars_per_hh +
            income_avg_k + pct_employed + pop_density_km2 + pct_age_0_14 +
            pct_owner_occupied + lbm_score | gemeente_code,
  data = df,
  vcov = ~gemeente_code
)

# ── Compare key coefficients across B, G, H ──────────────────────────────────
etable(mB, mG, mH,
       headers    = list("(B) Baseline interaction" = 1,
                         "(G) + Cars control"       = 1,
                         "(H) + Cars interaction"   = 1),
       keep       = c("prox_main", "pct_single_hh",
                      "prox_main:pct_single_hh",
                      "cars_per_hh",
                      "prox_main:cars_per_hh"),
       signif.code = c("***" = 0.001, "**" = 0.01, "*" = 0.05),
       notes = "Municipality FE, SEs clustered at gemeente level. Showing key coefficients only.")

cat("\nWithin-gemeente correlation: pct_single_hh vs cars_per_hh =",
    round(cor(
      df$pct_single_hh - ave(df$pct_single_hh, df$gemeente_code),
      df$cars_per_hh   - ave(df$cars_per_hh,   df$gemeente_code),
      use = "complete.obs"
    ), 3), "\n")
```

```{r cars-tipping-point}
# Conditional tipping point from Model H: cars_per_hh* = (-β1 - β3_singles*s̄) / β3_cars
# Evaluated at mean singles share — consistent with Table A6 formula
# ME = β1 + β3_singles*singles + β3_cars*cars = 0  →  solve for cars at singles = s̄

b1_h       <- coef(mH)["prox_main"]
b3_singles <- coef(mH)["prox_main:pct_single_hh"]
b3_cars    <- coef(mH)["prox_main:cars_per_hh"]
singles_mean <- mean(df$pct_single_hh, na.rm = TRUE)

v_h <- vcov(mH)[c("prox_main", "prox_main:pct_single_hh", "prox_main:cars_per_hh"),
                 c("prox_main", "prox_main:pct_single_hh", "prox_main:cars_per_hh")]

tp_h <- (-b1_h - b3_singles * singles_mean) / b3_cars

# Delta-method SE w.r.t. [β1, β3_singles, β3_cars]:
#   ∂tp/∂β1         = -1 / β3_cars
#   ∂tp/∂β3_singles = -s̄ / β3_cars
#   ∂tp/∂β3_cars    = (β1 + β3_singles*s̄) / β3_cars²
grad_h  <- c(-1 / b3_cars,
             -singles_mean / b3_cars,
             (b1_h + b3_singles * singles_mean) / b3_cars^2)
tp_h_se <- as.numeric(sqrt(t(grad_h) %*% v_h %*% grad_h))
tp_h_ci <- tp_h + c(-1.96, 1.96) * tp_h_se

cat("Model H — conditional tipping point (cars_per_hh*, at mean singles =",
    round(singles_mean, 1), "%):\n")
cat("Estimate:          ", round(tp_h, 3), "cars per household\n")
cat("95% CI:           [", round(tp_h_ci[1], 3), ",", round(tp_h_ci[2], 3), "]\n")
cat("Sample max cars:   ", round(max(df$cars_per_hh, na.rm = TRUE), 3), "\n")
cat("Sample 95th pct:   ", round(quantile(df$cars_per_hh, 0.95, na.rm = TRUE), 3), "\n")
cat("Tipping point within data range:", tp_h > 0 & tp_h < max(df$cars_per_hh, na.rm = TRUE), "\n")
```

```{r singles-tipping-point-modelH}
# In Model H, ME = β1 + β3_singles*singles + β3_cars*cars = 0
# Solving for singles*: singles* = (-β1 - β3_cars*cars_mean) / β3_singles
# Evaluated at mean and at selected cars_per_hh values

b1_H       <- coef(mH)["prox_main"]
b3_singles <- coef(mH)["prox_main:pct_single_hh"]
b3_cars    <- coef(mH)["prox_main:cars_per_hh"]
cars_mean  <- mean(df$cars_per_hh, na.rm = TRUE)
cars_med   <- median(df$cars_per_hh, na.rm = TRUE)

tp_singles_mean   <- (-b1_H - b3_cars * cars_mean)  / b3_singles
tp_singles_median <- (-b1_H - b3_cars * cars_med)   / b3_singles

# Delta-method SE at mean cars_per_hh
# tp = (-β1 - β3_cars*c) / β3_singles
# Gradient w.r.t. [β1, β3_singles, β3_cars]:
#   ∂tp/∂β1         = -1 / β3_singles
#   ∂tp/∂β3_singles = (β1 + β3_cars*c) / β3_singles²
#   ∂tp/∂β3_cars    = -c / β3_singles
v_H   <- vcov(mH)[c("prox_main", "prox_main:pct_single_hh", "prox_main:cars_per_hh"),
                   c("prox_main", "prox_main:pct_single_hh", "prox_main:cars_per_hh")]
c_val <- cars_mean
grad  <- c(
  -1 / b3_singles,
  (b1_H + b3_cars * c_val) / b3_singles^2,
  -c_val / b3_singles
)
tp_se <- as.numeric(sqrt(t(grad) %*% v_H %*% grad))
tp_ci <- tp_singles_mean + c(-1.96, 1.96) * tp_se

cat("Model H — singles tipping point (evaluated at mean cars_per_hh =",
    round(cars_mean, 2), "):\n")
cat("Estimate:                 ", round(tp_singles_mean, 1), "% single-HH share\n")
cat("95% CI:                  [", round(tp_ci[1], 1), ",", round(tp_ci[2], 1), "]\n")
cat("At median cars (", round(cars_med, 2), "):", round(tp_singles_median, 1), "%\n")
cat("Sample max singles:       ", round(max(df$pct_single_hh, na.rm = TRUE), 1), "%\n")
cat("Sample 95th pct singles:  ", round(quantile(df$pct_single_hh, 0.95, na.rm = TRUE), 1), "%\n")
cat("Within data range:        ", tp_singles_mean > 0 & tp_singles_mean < 100, "\n")
```

Two conditional tipping points are computed from Model H, each evaluated at the sample mean of the other moderator. The **conditional car ownership tipping point** (cars_per_hh\*) is the car ownership level at which the proximity discount disappears, evaluated at mean singles share (~34.3%). The **conditional singles tipping point** (pct_single_hh\*) is the singles share at which the proximity effect crosses zero, evaluated at mean car ownership (~1.17 cars/HH). Both use the delta method for confidence intervals and are directly comparable to the values reported in Table A6.

**Conditional cars tipping point (cars_per_hh\*):** evaluated at mean singles share (34.3%), the tipping point is **1.716 cars per household** (95% CI: 1.503–1.930). This is inside the observable data range (sample max 2.40, 95th percentile 1.60), meaning the flip from discount to neutrality genuinely occurs within Dutch data. The entire CI falls below the sample maximum and the lower bound (1.503) is within the top 5% of the distribution, making this a precisely identified and empirically credible threshold.

**Conditional singles tipping point (pct_single_hh\*):** evaluated at mean car ownership (1.17 cars/HH), the tipping point is **60.9%** (95% CI: 41–81%). This is inside the observable range (sample max 98%, 95th percentile 58%), meaning the flip from discount to premium genuinely occurs within Dutch data. The CI is entirely within 0–100%, a credible, precisely identified result. At median car ownership (1.20 cars/HH) the estimate is virtually identical (59.6%).

**Important caveat:** because Model H contains two interaction terms simultaneously, both tipping points are conditional, each threshold assumes the other moderator is held at its sample mean. Neither is a universal threshold; both are joint functions of demographics and mobility. This should be stated clearly in the thesis.

```{r fig-marginal-effects-modelH, fig.cap="Marginal effect of school distance on log WOZ by single-HH share and car ownership level. Shaded bands: 95% CI (gemeente-clustered)."}
library(ggplot2)

b1_H       <- coef(mH)["prox_main"]
b3_singles <- coef(mH)["prox_main:pct_single_hh"]
b3_cars    <- coef(mH)["prox_main:cars_per_hh"]
v_H        <- vcov(mH)[c("prox_main", "prox_main:pct_single_hh", "prox_main:cars_per_hh"),
                        c("prox_main", "prox_main:pct_single_hh", "prox_main:cars_per_hh")]

# Three representative car ownership levels (p10, mean, p90 for visible spread)
cars_levels <- c(
  "Low (p10)"    = unname(quantile(df$cars_per_hh, 0.10, na.rm = TRUE)),
  "Mean"         = unname(mean(df$cars_per_hh, na.rm = TRUE)),
  "High (p90)"   = unname(quantile(df$cars_per_hh, 0.90, na.rm = TRUE))
)

singles_seq <- seq(min(df$pct_single_hh, na.rm = TRUE),
                   max(df$pct_single_hh, na.rm = TRUE),
                   length.out = 200)

# Build data frame for all combinations
me_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(cars_levels), function(lbl) {
  c_val <- cars_levels[lbl]
  me    <- b1_H + b3_singles * singles_seq + b3_cars * c_val

  # Delta-method SE: Var(β1 + β3s*s + β3c*c)
  # Gradient w.r.t. [β1, β3_singles, β3_cars] = [1, s, c]
  se_me <- sapply(singles_seq, function(s) {
    g <- c(1, s, c_val)
    sqrt(as.numeric(t(g) %*% v_H %*% g))
  })

  data.frame(
    singles     = singles_seq,
    me          = me,
    lower       = me - 1.96 * se_me,
    upper       = me + 1.96 * se_me,
    cars_label  = lbl
  )
}))

me_df$cars_label <- factor(me_df$cars_label,
                            levels = c("Low (p10)", "Mean", "High (p90)"))

# Tipping points per car level (for vertical lines)
tp_df <- data.frame(
  cars_label = names(cars_levels),
  tp         = as.numeric((-b1_H - b3_cars * cars_levels) / b3_singles)
)
tp_df <- tp_df[tp_df$tp > 0 & tp_df$tp < 100, ]
tp_df$cars_label <- factor(tp_df$cars_label, levels = c("Low (p10)", "Mean", "High (p90)"))

ggplot(me_df, aes(x = singles, y = me,
                  colour = cars_label, fill = cars_label)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), alpha = 0.12, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(data = tp_df,
             aes(xintercept = tp, colour = cars_label),
             linetype = "dotted", linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c("Low (p10)" = "#1E7B4B", "Mean" = "#2E5D9E", "High (p90)" = "#C0392B"),
    name   = "Cars per household"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("Low (p10)" = "#1E7B4B", "Mean" = "#2E5D9E", "High (p90)" = "#C0392B"),
    name   = "Cars per household"
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Marginal effect of school distance on log WOZ",
    subtitle = "By single-HH share and car ownership level (Model H) | 95% CI | dotted lines = tipping points",
    x        = "Single-person household share (%)",
    y        = "ME of distance (km) on log WOZ"
  )

ggsave("output/figures/marginal_effects_modelH.png", width = 9, height = 5.5, dpi = 150)
```

The plot shows three lines corresponding to low (p10), mean, and high (p90) car ownership levels. Each line shows the marginal effect of school distance on log WOZ as a function of singles share, with 95% CI bands. Dotted vertical lines mark where each line crosses zero, the tipping point for that car ownership level.

All three lines have a negative slope (discount weakens as singles rise) and all cross zero within the observable data range. **Red (high car ownership, p90)** starts low (~0.06) and crosses zero earliest at ~42% singles. **Blue (mean car ownership)** crosses zero at ~61%. **Green (low car ownership, p10)** starts highest (~0.13) and crosses zero latest at ~81% singles.

The pattern is theoretically coherent: in high-car districts, proximity already matters less (lower starting discount), so a smaller demographic shift is enough to push the effect to zero. In low-car districts, the discount is larger but demographic composition needs to be more extreme to overcome it. The plot directly demonstrates why simpler models (A–D) found no tipping point — averaging across car ownership levels masks this heterogeneity.

```{r cars-twfe-models}
# ── Model I: TWFE + cars_per_hh as control (extends Model D) ─────────────────
m_twfe_I <- feols(
  log_woz ~ dist_primary_school * pct_single_hh +
            income_avg_k + pct_employed + pop_density_km2 + pct_age_0_14 +
            delta_singles_lag1 + pct_owner_occupied + lbm_score +
            cars_per_hh | wijk_code + year,
  data = panel_df,
  vcov = ~wijk_code
)

# ── Model J: TWFE + cars_per_hh as moderator ─────────────────────────────────
m_twfe_J <- feols(
  log_woz ~ dist_primary_school * pct_single_hh +
            dist_primary_school * cars_per_hh +
            income_avg_k + pct_employed + pop_density_km2 + pct_age_0_14 +
            delta_singles_lag1 + pct_owner_occupied + lbm_score | wijk_code + year,
  data = panel_df,
  vcov = ~wijk_code
)

etable(m_twfe_D, m_twfe_I, m_twfe_J,
       headers     = list("(D) TWFE baseline" = 1,
                          "(I) + Cars control" = 1,
                          "(J) + Cars interaction" = 1),
       keep        = c("dist_primary_school", "pct_single_hh",
                       "dist_primary_school:pct_single_hh",
                       "cars_per_hh",
                       "dist_primary_school:cars_per_hh"),
       signif.code = c("***" = 0.001, "**" = 0.01, "*" = 0.05),
       notes       = "District + year FE, SEs clustered at district level. Key coefficients only.")

cat("\nWithin-district correlation: pct_single_hh vs cars_per_hh =",
    round(cor(
      panel_df$pct_single_hh - ave(panel_df$pct_single_hh, panel_df$wijk_code),
      panel_df$cars_per_hh   - ave(panel_df$cars_per_hh,   panel_df$wijk_code),
      use = "complete.obs"
    ), 3), "\n")

# Save Extension 2 table as HTML + PNG (moved here so m_twfe_I and m_twfe_J exist)
ext2_tbl_args <- list(

                  "(H) Cars interaction (CS)"   = mH,

    "dist_primary_school:cars_per_hh"   = "Distance × Cars/HH",
    "income_avg_k"                      = "Avg. household income (k€)",

do.call(modelsummary, c(ext2_tbl_args, list(output = "output/tables/ext2_cars_table.html")))
webshot2::webshot("output/tables/ext2_cars_table.html",

                  zoom = 2)
```

Models I and J are the panel equivalents of G and H, they add car ownership to the TWFE specification to test whether the cross-sectional car ownership finding survives the stricter within-district identification.

**Model I (cars as control):** the proximity coefficient barely changes (0.046 → 0.044). Car ownership does not absorb the proximity discount in the panel either. `cars_per_hh` is positive and significant (+0.053\*): within districts over time, gaining more cars is associated with higher WOZ, even after absorbing permanent district characteristics.

**Model J (cars as moderator):** `dist_primary_school × cars_per_hh` is −0.044 (p = 0.19) — not significant. The car ownership interaction does not survive the panel test. The within-district correlation between `pct_single_hh` and `cars_per_hh` is only −0.354 (much lower than the cross-sectional −0.741), so multicollinearity is not the reason. The most likely explanation is that Dutch car ownership changes very slowly within districts over 6 years, the panel simply lacks sufficient within-district variation in car ownership to identify the interaction effect. Car ownership is a slow-moving structural characteristic, and the cross-sectional finding from Model H should be interpreted as a structural relationship across districts rather than a causal within-district effect.

# Full Results Table (Paper-Ready)

This section produces the consolidated regression table covering all ten specifications (Models A–J), formatted for direct inclusion in the paper. The table groups models into five blocks: cross-sectional main results (A–B), panel TWFE (C–D), school quality extension (E–F), car ownership cross-section (G–H), and car ownership panel (I–J). Fixed effect structure and sample are indicated via custom rows and the footnote.

The table uses `modelsummary` with `kableExtra` for HTML rendering. All distance variables from different models are mapped to the same label ("Distance to school") so rows align across model types. The `plyr`/`modelsummary` namespace conflict is resolved by detaching `plyr` if loaded.

```{r full-table-prep, include=FALSE}
# ── Ensure all model objects exist before building the full table ─────────────
# mE and mF are created inside an if(has_quality) block in school-quality-models.
# If that block was skipped (e.g. dist_good_school_km not yet in df), recreate them here.

if (!exists("mE") || !exists("mF")) {
  # Try to load quality distances from spatial_vars.rds and merge onto df
  if (file.exists("data/processed/spatial_vars.rds")) {
    sv <- readRDS("data/processed/spatial_vars.rds")
    if (all(c("dist_good_school_km", "dist_std_school_km") %in% names(sv))) {
      df <- df %>%
        select(-any_of(c("dist_good_school_km", "dist_std_school_km"))) %>%
        left_join(sv %>% select(wijk_code, dist_good_school_km, dist_std_school_km),
                  by = "wijk_code")
      message("Quality distances loaded from spatial_vars.rds for table prep.")
    }
  }

  # Only estimate if columns are now available in df
  if (all(c("dist_good_school_km", "dist_std_school_km") %in% names(df))) {
    mE <- feols(
      log_woz ~ dist_good_school_km * pct_single_hh +
                income_avg_k + pct_employed + pop_density_km2 + pct_age_0_14 +
                pct_owner_occupied + lbm_score | gemeente_code,
      data = df, vcov = ~gemeente_code
    )
    mF <- feols(
      log_woz ~ dist_std_school_km * pct_single_hh +
                income_avg_k + pct_employed + pop_density_km2 + pct_age_0_14 +
                pct_owner_occupied + lbm_score | gemeente_code,
      data = df, vcov = ~gemeente_code
    )
    message("mE and mF recreated in full-table-prep.")
  } else {
    stop("dist_good_school_km not available in df. Re-run the school-quality-distances chunk to rebuild spatial_vars.rds, then knit again.")
  }
}

# Ensure car ownership models exist
if (!exists("mG")) {
```

**Why no TWFE model with control for school quality?**

Models E–F use a 2023 cross-section because school quality distances are derived from a single DUO snapshot; a panel extension would require year-by-year school geocoding and is left for future work.

The full structure of the analysis is: cross-sectional Models A/B and panel Models C/D as the **main results** testing H1–H3; Models E/F (school quality split) and Models G–J (car ownership) as **extensions** introducing new theoretical mechanisms; and the robustness checks in the following section validating the main results across alternative samples and proximity operationalisations.

---

# Robustness Checks

Three robustness checks are applied to both the preferred cross-sectional specification (Model B) and the car ownership interaction model (Model H), which contains the main new finding. For each check the key coefficients are reported in a compact summary table.

The four checks are:

1. **Alternative proximity measure (sensitivity)** — replace `prox_main` (CBS-reported average distance) with `dist_school_centroid_km` (centroid-to-nearest-school distance computed via DUO spatial join). Because the two measures correlate only at r = 0.576, differences in results reflect the conceptual gap between address-based and centroid-based distance rather than model fragility, this check is therefore labelled a sensitivity check rather than a strict robustness check.
2. **Stricter population threshold** — raise the minimum population from 500 to 1,000 residents, dropping smaller districts whose WOZ averages are less reliable.
3. **Excluding the four largest cities** — drop Amsterdam (GM0363), Rotterdam (GM0599), Den Haag (GM0518), and Utrecht (GM0344), which dominate the high-singles tail and could be driving the interaction results.
4. **Alternative proximity operationalisation (density)** — replace the distance variable with `n_schools_1km`, the number of primary schools within 1 km of the wijk centroid. The 1 km radius is chosen because it is close to the mean CBS distance (~0.91 km). Note the expected sign reversal: a negative coefficient on `n_schools_1km` is the density-model equivalent of a positive distance coefficient (both indicate a proximity discount).

```{r robustness-setup}
# ── Shared formula components ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
controls_B <- "income_avg_k + pct_employed + pop_density_km2 + pct_age_0_14 +
               pct_owner_occupied + lbm_score"

controls_H <- "income_avg_k + pct_employed + pop_density_km2 + pct_age_0_14 +
               pct_owner_occupied + lbm_score"

big4 <- c("GM0363", "GM0599", "GM0518", "GM0344")  # Amsterdam, Rotterdam, Den Haag, Utrecht

# ── Sample variants ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
df_pop1000  <- df %>% filter(pop_total > 1000)
df_nobig4   <- df %>% filter(!gemeente_code %in% big4)
```

```{r robustness-modelB}
# ── Model B: baseline (already estimated, repeated here for reference) ────────
# mB — main sample, CBS distance, pop > 500

# B-rob1: centroid distance instead of CBS distance
mB_rob1 <- feols(
  log_woz ~ dist_school_centroid_km * pct_single_hh +
            income_avg_k + pct_employed + pop_density_km2 + pct_age_0_14 +
            pct_owner_occupied + lbm_score | gemeente_code,
  data = df,
  vcov = ~gemeente_code
)

# B-rob2: pop > 1000
mB_rob2 <- feols(
  log_woz ~ prox_main * pct_single_hh +
            income_avg_k + pct_employed + pop_density_km2 + pct_age_0_14 +
            pct_owner_occupied + lbm_score | gemeente_code,
  data = df_pop1000,
  vcov = ~gemeente_code
)

# B-rob3: exclude big 4 cities
mB_rob3 <- feols(
  log_woz ~ prox_main * pct_single_hh +
            income_avg_k + pct_employed + pop_density_km2 + pct_age_0_14 +
            pct_owner_occupied + lbm_score | gemeente_code,
  data = df_nobig4,
  vcov = ~gemeente_code
)

# B-dens: school density within 1km (alternative proximity operationalisation)
mB_dens <- feols(
  log_woz ~ n_schools_1km * pct_single_hh +
            income_avg_k + pct_employed + pop_density_km2 + pct_age_0_14 +
            pct_owner_occupied + lbm_score | gemeente_code,
  data = df,
  vcov = ~gemeente_code
)

etable(mB, mB_rob1, mB_rob2, mB_rob3, mB_dens,
       headers     = list("(B) Baseline"       = 1,
                          "(B-r1) Centroid"    = 1,
                          "(B-r2) Pop > 1000"  = 1,
                          "(B-r3) No big 4"    = 1,
                          "(B-dens) Density"   = 1),
       keep        = c("prox_main", "dist_school_centroid_km", "n_schools_1km",
                       "pct_single_hh",
                       "prox_main:pct_single_hh",
                       "dist_school_centroid_km:pct_single_hh",
                       "n_schools_1km:pct_single_hh"),
       signif.code = c("***" = 0.001, "**" = 0.01, "*" = 0.05),
       notes       = "Municipality FE, SEs clustered at gemeente level. Key coefficients only. B-dens uses school count within 1km — sign reversal expected.")
```

The Model B robustness results are reassuring across all four checks:

**B-r1 (Centroid distance — sensitivity check):** `dist_school_centroid_km` is positive and significant (0.028\*), same direction as the CBS measure. The interaction with singles is −0.0003, same sign but smaller. Note that the correlation between the two distance measures is only r = 0.576 (see Appendix), so this is better treated as a sensitivity check than a strict robustness check — differences in results reflect the conceptual gap between centroid-based and address-based distance rather than fragility of the finding.

**B-r2 (Pop > 1000):** Results are almost identical to baseline — `prox_main` 0.049\*\*, `pct_single_hh` −0.004\*\*\*. If anything slightly stronger. The results are not driven by small, unreliable districts.

**B-r3 (No big 4 cities):** Very stable — `prox_main` 0.053\*\*, `pct_single_hh` −0.003\*. Excluding Amsterdam, Rotterdam, Den Haag and Utrecht barely changes anything. The proximity discount and negative singles effect are not an urban big-city phenomenon.

**B-dens (School density within 1km):** `n_schools_1km` is −0.021\*\*\* — negative and highly significant, directly replicating the proximity discount with the expected sign reversal (more schools nearby = lower WOZ). The interaction `n_schools_1km:pct_single_hh` is +0.0004\*\*\* — positive and significant, meaning the density discount weakens as singles share rises. This is actually stronger confirmation of H2 than the distance-based Model B itself, suggesting the density measure picks up the demographic moderating channel more cleanly. The correlation between `n_schools_1km` and `dist_primary_school` is −0.398 (see Appendix), confirming the two operationalisations capture related but meaningfully different aspects of proximity.

**One honest note across all checks:** the `prox_main:pct_single_hh` interaction remains insignificant in B-r1 through B-r3. The singles interaction only becomes significant once car ownership is jointly modelled (Model H) or when school density is used instead of distance (B-dens).

**Bottom line:** the two core Model B findings — proximity is a discount and higher singles share lowers WOZ — are robust across all four checks.

```{r robustness-modelH}
# ── Model H: car ownership interaction ────────────────────────────────────────
# mH — main sample, CBS distance, pop > 500

# H-rob1: centroid distance instead of CBS distance
mH_rob1 <- feols(
  log_woz ~ dist_school_centroid_km * pct_single_hh +
            dist_school_centroid_km * cars_per_hh +
            income_avg_k + pct_employed + pop_density_km2 + pct_age_0_14 +
            pct_owner_occupied + lbm_score | gemeente_code,
  data = df,
  vcov = ~gemeente_code
)

# H-rob2: pop > 1000
mH_rob2 <- feols(
  log_woz ~ prox_main * pct_single_hh +
            prox_main * cars_per_hh +
            income_avg_k + pct_employed + pop_density_km2 + pct_age_0_14 +
            pct_owner_occupied + lbm_score | gemeente_code,
  data = df_pop1000,
  vcov = ~gemeente_code
)

# H-rob3: exclude big 4 cities
mH_rob3 <- feols(
  log_woz ~ prox_main * pct_single_hh +
            prox_main * cars_per_hh +
            income_avg_k + pct_employed + pop_density_km2 + pct_age_0_14 +
            pct_owner_occupied + lbm_score | gemeente_code,
  data = df_nobig4,
  vcov = ~gemeente_code
)

# H-dens: school density within 1km (alternative proximity operationalisation)
mH_dens <- feols(
  log_woz ~ n_schools_1km * pct_single_hh +
            n_schools_1km * cars_per_hh +
            income_avg_k + pct_employed + pop_density_km2 + pct_age_0_14 +
            pct_owner_occupied + lbm_score | gemeente_code,
  data = df,
  vcov = ~gemeente_code
)

etable(mH, mH_rob1, mH_rob2, mH_rob3, mH_dens,
       headers     = list("(H) Baseline"       = 1,
                          "(H-r1) Centroid"    = 1,
                          "(H-r2) Pop > 1000"  = 1,
                          "(H-r3) No big 4"    = 1,
                          "(H-dens) Density"   = 1),
       keep        = c("prox_main", "dist_school_centroid_km", "n_schools_1km",
                       "pct_single_hh",
                       "prox_main:pct_single_hh",
                       "dist_school_centroid_km:pct_single_hh",
                       "n_schools_1km:pct_single_hh",
                       "cars_per_hh",
                       "prox_main:cars_per_hh",
                       "dist_school_centroid_km:cars_per_hh",
                       "n_schools_1km:cars_per_hh"),
       signif.code = c("***" = 0.001, "**" = 0.01, "*" = 0.05),
       notes       = "Municipality FE, SEs clustered at gemeente level. Key coefficients only. H-dens uses school count within 1km — sign reversal expected.")
```

Model H robustness gives a mixed but informative picture across four checks:

**H-r1 (Centroid distance — sensitivity check):** Both interactions lose significance — `dist_school_centroid_km:cars_per_hh` is +0.009 (wrong sign, not significant). The centroid-based measure does not replicate Model H's findings. As with B-r1, this reflects the conceptual difference between the two distance measures (r = 0.576) rather than pure fragility — the CBS address-based distance is the theoretically superior measure for capturing the residential experience of households.

**H-r2 (Pop > 1000):** `prox_main` stays positive and significant (0.157\*), `prox_main:cars_per_hh` drops to −0.059 (p ≈ 0.10, marginally insignificant). The singles interaction also weakens. The stricter population filter reduces the sample by ~308 districts and precision drops — the direction is consistent but significance is lost.

**H-r3 (No big 4 cities):** The strongest confirmation. `prox_main` 0.230\*\*\*, `prox_main:cars_per_hh` −0.094\*\*\*, `prox_main:pct_single_hh` −0.002\*\*\* — all three key coefficients match the baseline almost exactly. The four largest cities are not driving Model H's findings.

**H-dens (School density within 1km):** `n_schools_1km:cars_per_hh` is −0.023\*\*\* — significant, but the direction implies a different mechanism than Model H. In the density model, a negative density×cars coefficient means the school density discount is *larger* in high-car districts, suggesting car-driving households are more sensitive to the congestion and noise of multiple nearby schools. This is distinct from the distance-based finding (where car ownership weakens the discount) and reflects a genuine conceptual difference between density and distance as proximity measures — they are not interchangeable robustness checks for Model H.

**Overall verdict:** Model H is **partially robust**. The car ownership interaction survives the big-city exclusion (H-r3) and shows a consistent direction in the density check (H-dens), but is sensitive to the distance operationalisation and weakens under stricter population restrictions. This partial robustness should be reported honestly — the finding is credible but not universal across all specifications.

```{r robustness-tipping-points-singles}
# Singles tipping point (pct_single_hh*) across Model H robustness checks
# Formula: singles* = (-β1 - β3_cars * cars_mean) / β3_singles
# Evaluated at mean cars_per_hh of the respective sample

rob_models_H <- list(
  "H baseline"    = list(mod = mH,      dv = "prox_main",               data = df),
  "H-r1 Centroid" = list(mod = mH_rob1, dv = "dist_school_centroid_km", data = df),
  "H-r2 Pop>1000" = list(mod = mH_rob2, dv = "prox_main",               data = df_pop1000),
  "H-r3 No big 4" = list(mod = mH_rob3, dv = "prox_main",               data = df_nobig4)
)

singles_tp_results <- lapply(names(rob_models_H), function(nm) {
  m      <- rob_models_H[[nm]]$mod
  dv     <- rob_models_H[[nm]]$dv
  d      <- rob_models_H[[nm]]$data
  c_mean <- mean(d$cars_per_hh, na.rm = TRUE)

  b1      <- tryCatch(coef(m)[dv],                              error = function(e) NA)
  b3_sing <- tryCatch(coef(m)[paste0(dv, ":pct_single_hh")],   error = function(e) NA)
  b3_cars <- tryCatch(coef(m)[paste0(dv, ":cars_per_hh")],     error = function(e) NA)

  if (any(is.na(c(b1, b3_sing, b3_cars))) || b3_sing == 0)
    return(data.frame(spec = nm, tp = NA, lower = NA, upper = NA,
                      cars_mean = round(c_mean, 3), in_range = NA))

  tp <- (-b1 - b3_cars * c_mean) / b3_sing

  # Delta-method SE w.r.t. [β1, β3_singles, β3_cars]
  v    <- vcov(m)[c(dv, paste0(dv, ":pct_single_hh"), paste0(dv, ":cars_per_hh")),
                   c(dv, paste0(dv, ":pct_single_hh"), paste0(dv, ":cars_per_hh"))]
  grad <- c(-1/b3_sing,
            (b1 + b3_cars * c_mean) / b3_sing^2,
            -c_mean / b3_sing)
  se   <- sqrt(as.numeric(t(grad) %*% v %*% grad))
  ci   <- tp + c(-1.96, 1.96) * se

  data.frame(spec      = nm,
             tp        = round(tp, 1),
             lower     = round(ci[1], 1),
             upper     = round(ci[2], 1),
             cars_mean = round(c_mean, 3),
             in_range  = tp > 0 & tp < 100)
})

singles_tp_df <- do.call(rbind, singles_tp_results)

cat("Singles tipping point (pct_single_hh*) across Model H robustness checks:\n\n")
print(singles_tp_df, row.names = FALSE)
cat("\nSample 95th pct singles:", round(quantile(df$pct_single_hh, 0.95, na.rm = TRUE), 1), "%\n")
cat("Sample max singles:     ", round(max(df$pct_single_hh, na.rm = TRUE), 1), "%\n")
```

The table demonstrates:

**H baseline: 60.9% [41.0, 80.7]** — the main result, tight CI entirely within 0–100%, `in_range = TRUE`. 

**H-r1 Centroid: 74.5% [−55.5, 204.5]** — the point estimate is within range but the CI is enormous and crosses both 0 and 100. This reflects that the underlying interactions are not significant with centroid distance — the tipping point exists in the formula but is not statistically credible. Discard.

**H-r2 Pop > 1000: 93.7% [−13.3, 200.7]** — point estimate shifts to 93.7% but with a very wide CI that crosses zero. Again, the weaker significance of the interactions in the restricted sample makes the tipping point imprecise. Directionally consistent but not significant.

**H-r3 No big 4: 56.8% [40.3, 73.3]** — almost identical to baseline, tight CI, entirely within range. The best robustness confirmation — excluding the four largest cities gives 56.8% vs 60.9%, overlapping CIs, both precise. 

**The honest summary for the thesis:**

The singles tipping point is **robust only in the no-big-4 check** (56.8%, CI [40.3, 73.3]). The pop > 1000 and centroid checks produce wide CIs due to weaker underlying interactions. Combined with H-r3, you can credibly say:

*"The conditional singles tipping point of ~61% is stable when excluding the four largest cities (56.8%, CI [40.3, 73.3]) but becomes imprecise under stricter population restrictions and alternative distance measures, reflecting the partial robustness of the car ownership interaction documented in Table A6."*

This is an honest and defensible conclusion — the finding is real but not universal across all specifications.

```{r robustness-tipping-points-cars}
# Conditional tipping points (cars_per_hh*) for Model H robustness variants
# Formula: cars* = (-β1 - β3_singles*s̄) / β3_cars  — consistent with Table A6
# Each variant uses the mean singles share of its own sample

rob_models_cars <- list(
  "H baseline"    = list(mod = mH,      dv = "prox_main",               data = df),
  "H-r1 Centroid" = list(mod = mH_rob1, dv = "dist_school_centroid_km", data = df),
  "H-r2 Pop>1000" = list(mod = mH_rob2, dv = "prox_main",               data = df_pop1000),
  "H-r3 No big 4" = list(mod = mH_rob3, dv = "prox_main",               data = df_nobig4)
)

rob_tp <- lapply(names(rob_models_cars), function(nm) {
  m      <- rob_models_cars[[nm]]$mod
  dv     <- rob_models_cars[[nm]]$dv
  d      <- rob_models_cars[[nm]]$data
  s_mean <- mean(d$pct_single_hh, na.rm = TRUE)

  b1      <- tryCatch(coef(m)[dv],                              error = function(e) NA)
  b3_sing <- tryCatch(coef(m)[paste0(dv, ":pct_single_hh")],   error = function(e) NA)
  b3_cars <- tryCatch(coef(m)[paste0(dv, ":cars_per_hh")],     error = function(e) NA)

  if (any(is.na(c(b1, b3_sing, b3_cars))) || b3_cars == 0)
    return(c(tp = NA, lower = NA, upper = NA))

  tp <- (-b1 - b3_sing * s_mean) / b3_cars

  # Delta-method SE w.r.t. [β1, β3_singles, β3_cars]
  v    <- vcov(m)[c(dv, paste0(dv, ":pct_single_hh"), paste0(dv, ":cars_per_hh")),
                  c(dv, paste0(dv, ":pct_single_hh"), paste0(dv, ":cars_per_hh"))]
  grad <- c(-1/b3_cars, -s_mean/b3_cars, (b1 + b3_sing * s_mean)/b3_cars^2)
  se   <- sqrt(as.numeric(t(grad) %*% v %*% grad))
  c(tp = round(tp, 3), lower = round(tp - 1.96*se, 3), upper = round(tp + 1.96*se, 3))
})

cat("Cars tipping point (cars_per_hh*, conditional on mean singles) across Model H robustness checks:\n\n")
tp_summary <- do.call(rbind, rob_tp)
rownames(tp_summary) <- names(rob_models_cars)
print(tp_summary)
cat("\nSample max cars_per_hh:", round(max(df$cars_per_hh, na.rm = TRUE), 3), "\n")
```

Very informative — and consistent with what we saw in the model table. All values are now the conditional tipping point (at mean singles of the respective sample), matching the formula used in Table A6.

**H baseline: 1.716 [1.503, 1.930]** — the main result, matching the value reported in the `cars-tipping-point` chunk. Tight CI, entirely within the data range (sample max 2.40).

**H-r1 Centroid: −0.419 [−8.285, 7.447]** — meaningless. The negative point estimate and enormous CI confirm the underlying interactions are not identified with centroid distance. Discard.

**H-r2 Pop > 1000: 2.089 [1.003, 3.174]** — shifts upward to 2.09, CI widens as expected with fewer observations, but the lower bound (1.003) is within the data range. Directionally consistent, less precise.

**H-r3 No big 4: 1.718 [1.515, 1.921]** — virtually identical to the baseline (1.716 vs 1.718), with essentially the same CI. The strongest confirmation — removing the four largest cities changes nothing.

**The honest thesis summary of all robustness:**

The conditional cars tipping point is **stable at ~1.72–2.09 cars/HH** across the two meaningful checks (pop > 1000 and no big 4), with overlapping confidence intervals. It is not identified when using the centroid distance measure. The finding is robust to sample composition but tied to the CBS distance operationalisation — which should be acknowledged as a limitation.

A clean one-sentence thesis statement: *"The conditional car ownership tipping point of 1.716 cars per household is stable across sample restrictions (2.089 with pop > 1000; 1.718 excluding the four largest cities) but cannot be identified using the centroid-based distance measure, suggesting sensitivity to the proximity operationalisation."*

Note: the school density check (B-dens, H-dens) is not included in the tipping point stability analysis. The density model replaces distance with school count, reversing the sign of the main effect and changing what the interaction term captures — a tipping point derived from `mH_dens` would not be directly comparable to the 1.716 cars/HH and 60.9% singles estimates from the distance-based Model H, and including it would conflate two different mechanisms rather than providing a genuine stability check.
