```{r tipping-point-table}
# ── Table A6: Implied tipping points across robustness specifications ──────────
# Helper: format tp + CI as "X.X% [lo, hi]" or "—" if NA / not identified
fmt_tp <- function(tp, lo, hi, pct = FALSE) {
  if (is.na(tp)) return("&mdash;")
  sfx <- if (pct) "%" else ""
  sprintf("%.1f%s [%.1f, %.1f]", tp, sfx, lo, hi)
}

# ── Model B: singles tipping point only (no cars interaction) ─────────────────
b_specs <- list(
  "(B) Baseline"    = list(mod = mB,      dv = "prox_main"),
  "(B-r1) Centroid" = list(mod = mB_rob1, dv = "dist_school_centroid_km"),
  "(B-r2) Pop>1000" = list(mod = mB_rob2, dv = "prox_main"),
  "(B-r3) No big 4" = list(mod = mB_rob3, dv = "prox_main")
)

b_tp_rows <- lapply(names(b_specs), function(nm) {
  m       <- b_specs[[nm]]$mod
  dv      <- b_specs[[nm]]$dv
  b1      <- tryCatch(coef(m)[dv],                            error = function(e) NA)
  b3_sing <- tryCatch(coef(m)[paste0(dv, ":pct_single_hh")], error = function(e) NA)
  if (any(is.na(c(b1, b3_sing))) || b3_sing == 0)
    return(data.frame(spec = nm, singles_fmt = "&mdash;", cars_fmt = "&mdash;",
                      stringsAsFactors = FALSE))
  tp   <- -b1 / b3_sing
  v    <- vcov(m)[c(dv, paste0(dv, ":pct_single_hh")),
                  c(dv, paste0(dv, ":pct_single_hh"))]
  grad <- c(-1/b3_sing, b1/b3_sing^2)
  se   <- sqrt(as.numeric(t(grad) %*% v %*% grad))
  ci   <- tp + c(-1.96, 1.96) * se
  data.frame(spec       = nm,
             singles_fmt = fmt_tp(tp, ci[1], ci[2], pct = TRUE),
             cars_fmt    = "&mdash;",
             stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
})
b_tp <- do.call(rbind, b_tp_rows)

# ── Model H: singles tipping point (from earlier chunk) + cars recomputed ─────
h_specs_list <- list(
  "(H) Baseline"    = list(mod = mH,      dv = "prox_main",               data = df),
  "(H-r1) Centroid" = list(mod = mH_rob1, dv = "dist_school_centroid_km", data = df),
  "(H-r2) Pop>1000" = list(mod = mH_rob2, dv = "prox_main",               data = df_pop1000),
  "(H-r3) No big 4" = list(mod = mH_rob3, dv = "prox_main",               data = df_nobig4)
)

h_tp_rows <- lapply(names(h_specs_list), function(nm) {
  m        <- h_specs_list[[nm]]$mod
  dv       <- h_specs_list[[nm]]$dv
  d        <- h_specs_list[[nm]]$data
  c_mean   <- mean(d$cars_per_hh,   na.rm = TRUE)
  s_mean   <- mean(d$pct_single_hh, na.rm = TRUE)

  b1      <- tryCatch(coef(m)[dv],                                    error = function(e) NA)
  b3_sing <- tryCatch(coef(m)[paste0(dv, ":pct_single_hh")],         error = function(e) NA)
  b3_cars <- tryCatch(coef(m)[paste0(dv, ":cars_per_hh")],           error = function(e) NA)

  # Singles tipping point at mean cars
  sing_fmt <- tryCatch({
    if (any(is.na(c(b1, b3_sing, b3_cars))) || b3_sing == 0) return("&mdash;")
    tp   <- (-b1 - b3_cars * c_mean) / b3_sing
    v    <- vcov(m)[c(dv, paste0(dv, ":pct_single_hh"), paste0(dv, ":cars_per_hh")),
                    c(dv, paste0(dv, ":pct_single_hh"), paste0(dv, ":cars_per_hh"))]
    grad <- c(-1/b3_sing, (b1 + b3_cars*c_mean)/b3_sing^2, -c_mean/b3_sing)
    se   <- sqrt(as.numeric(t(grad) %*% v %*% grad))
    ci   <- tp + c(-1.96, 1.96) * se
    fmt_tp(tp, ci[1], ci[2], pct = TRUE)
  }, error = function(e) "&mdash;")

  # Cars tipping point at mean singles
  cars_fmt <- tryCatch({
    if (any(is.na(c(b1, b3_sing, b3_cars))) || b3_cars == 0) return("&mdash;")
    tp   <- (-b1 - b3_sing * s_mean) / b3_cars
    v    <- vcov(m)[c(dv, paste0(dv, ":pct_single_hh"), paste0(dv, ":cars_per_hh")),
                    c(dv, paste0(dv, ":pct_single_hh"), paste0(dv, ":cars_per_hh"))]
    grad <- c(-1/b3_cars, -s_mean/b3_cars, (b1 + b3_sing*s_mean)/b3_cars^2)
    se   <- sqrt(as.numeric(t(grad) %*% v %*% grad))
    ci   <- tp + c(-1.96, 1.96) * se
    fmt_tp(tp, ci[1], ci[2], pct = FALSE)
  }, error = function(e) "&mdash;")

  data.frame(spec = nm, singles_fmt = sing_fmt, cars_fmt = cars_fmt,
             stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
})
h_tp <- do.call(rbind, h_tp_rows)

# ── Combine and render ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
tp_combined        <- rbind(b_tp, h_tp)
colnames(tp_combined) <- c("Specification",
                            "Singles tipping point [95% CI]",
                            "Cars/HH tipping point [95% CI]")

tbl_tp <- knitr::kable(
  tp_combined,
  format  = "html",
  caption = "Table A6. Implied tipping points across robustness specifications",
  align   = c("l", "c", "c"),
  escape  = FALSE
) %>%
  kable_styling(
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"),
    full_width        = FALSE,
    font_size         = 13,
    html_font         = "Times New Roman, Times, serif"
  ) %>%
  pack_rows("Model B — cross-sectional baseline (no car interaction)", 1, 4) %>%
  pack_rows("Model H — car ownership interaction", 5, 8) %>%
  add_footnote(
    label    = "Singles tipping point: single-HH share (%) at which the marginal distance effect equals zero, evaluated at the sample mean of cars per household. Cars tipping point: cars per household at which the marginal distance effect equals zero. '—' indicates no interaction term present. 95% CIs computed via the delta method. Density variants (B-dens, H-dens) excluded as the school-count operationalisation reverses the sign of the proximity effect, making tipping points non-comparable. * p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001.",
    notation = "none"
  )

tbl_tp %>% save_kable("output/tables/tipping_point_table.html", self_contained = TRUE)
webshot2::webshot("output/tables/tipping_point_table.html",
                  "output/figures/tipping_point_table.png", zoom = 2)
```

# Appendix

## Proximity Measure Validation

Before relying on `dist_primary_school` (CBS) as the main proximity variable, it is worth verifying how closely it aligns with `dist_school_centroid_km` (our own centroid-based measure computed from DUO coordinates). A strong correlation between the two confirms that the CBS-reported distances are well-behaved and that our spatial join is consistent with the official data. A weak correlation would signal measurement differences worth investigating.

```{r proximity-measure-correlation, fig.cap="Correlation between CBS-reported distance and centroid-based distance to nearest primary school."}
# ── Compute correlation ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
cor_val <- cor(df$dist_primary_school, df$dist_school_centroid_km,
               use = "complete.obs")
n_both  <- sum(!is.na(df$dist_primary_school) & !is.na(df$dist_school_centroid_km))

cat("Pearson correlation: r =", round(cor_val, 3), "\n")
cat("N (both measures available):", n_both, "\n")
cat("Mean CBS distance:      ", round(mean(df$dist_primary_school,      na.rm = TRUE), 3), "km\n")
cat("Mean centroid distance: ", round(mean(df$dist_school_centroid_km,  na.rm = TRUE), 3), "km\n")

# ── Scatter plot ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ggplot(df, aes(x = dist_primary_school, y = dist_school_centroid_km)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25, size = 0.8, colour = "#2E5D9E") +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0,
              linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "#E07B39", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.5, y = max(df$dist_school_centroid_km, na.rm = TRUE) * 0.9,
           label = paste0("r = ", round(cor_val, 3)),
           size = 4.5, colour = "#2E5D9E") +
  labs(
    title    = "CBS distance vs centroid-based distance to nearest primary school",
    subtitle = "Dashed line = perfect agreement (slope 1, intercept 0) | Orange = OLS fit",
    x        = "CBS average distance to school (km)",
    y        = "Centroid-to-nearest-school distance (km)"
  )

ggsave("output/figures/proximity_measure_correlation.png", width = 9, height = 5.5, dpi = 150)
```

r = 0.576 is lower than ideal — this deserves careful interpretation. Several factors explain it:

**1. Fundamentally different measurement concepts**
The CBS measure (`dist_primary_school`) is the **average distance from all residential addresses** in the wijk to their nearest school. The centroid measure (`dist_school_centroid_km`) is the distance from the **geometric centre of the wijk polygon** to the nearest school. These are conceptually different things. In a wijk where residents cluster near one edge (e.g. along a river or motorway), the centroid can be very far from where most people actually live, creating large discrepancies.

**2. The vertical striping you see in the plot**
The CBS values are rounded to one decimal place (0.3, 0.4, 0.5 km...), which creates the vertical stripes. For each CBS value, the centroid measure varies widely — some wijken with CBS distance 0.5 km have centroid distances anywhere from 0 to 3+ km. This inflates scatter and depresses correlation.

**3. Mean CBS (0.913 km) > Mean centroid (0.796 km)**
The OLS line sitting below the 45° dashed line confirms this systematic difference. CBS averages across all addresses, many of which are on the outskirts of the wijk and therefore further from schools. The centroid is a single central point which tends to be closer to schools than the average residential address in spread-out wijken.

**4. Large wijken cause the most divergence**
Rural and suburban wijken are both geographically large and irregularly shaped — their centroids can be far from the population concentration, causing the largest discrepancies visible in the upper-left area of the plot.

**What this means for the thesis:**

r = 0.576 is actually a reasonable finding that you should report honestly. The two measures capture related but distinct aspects of proximity. This explains why the robustness check with centroid distance (H-r1) gave different results from the CBS-based models — the two variables are not interchangeable, and the CBS measure is theoretically superior for this analysis because it reflects the actual residential experience of households in the wijk rather than an arbitrary geometric point.

In the thesis you can write: *"The CBS-reported average distance and the centroid-based distance are moderately correlated (r = 0.576), reflecting that the two operationalisations capture related but distinct aspects of school proximity. The CBS measure is preferred as it is based on actual residential addresses rather than the geometric centroid of the district polygon, which may fall far from the population concentration in large or irregularly shaped wijken."*

## Correlation Between Distance and Density Proximity Measures

The robustness check using `n_schools_1km` (school density within 1 km) as an alternative proximity operationalisation rests on the assumption that the two measures — distance to nearest school and number of schools nearby — are related but not identical. A high positive correlation would make the density check redundant; a very low correlation would raise concerns about whether they measure the same underlying concept at all. The correlation below quantifies this relationship and informs how to interpret the density robustness results.

```{r correlation-of-n_schools_1km-and-dist_primary_school}
cat("Correlation between n_schools_1km and dist_primary_school:\n")
cat("r =", round(cor(df$n_schools_1km, df$dist_primary_school, use = "complete.obs"), 3), "\n")
cat("\nNote: negative correlation expected — more schools nearby = shorter distance to nearest school.")
```

The correlation is negative as expected (more schools within 1 km → shorter distance to the nearest school) but only moderate in magnitude (r ≈ −0.40). This confirms that the two operationalisations overlap partially but capture meaningfully different aspects of school proximity: distance captures how far the nearest school is, while density captures how many schools are within walking distance. The moderate correlation justifies including the density check as a genuine alternative perspective — it is neither redundant (too correlated) nor disconnected (too different).
